hypotheses.result_summary: Implemented and ran (experiments/quality_latency_joint.csv, 94 rows). Only 6 of results.csv's rows have both a chrf_score AND a joinable latency metric (the asr_keyterms_on/off/on2/off2/on3/off3 family, all sharing wjZofJX0v4M 5:00-15:00) -- every other chrF-scored row predates the event-logging schema the CLA/flicker/decomposition scripts all depend on, or every other event-logged row was never scored for chrF. This IS the joint table papi2025-howreal calls for, but its immediate value this cycle is exposing how THIN the overlap between 'has quality score' and 'has fine-grained latency breakdown' actually is in this repo's existing 94 experiments, rather than revealing a new tradeoff among those 6 rows (which differ mainly in an old keyterm on/off toggle already analyzed elsewhere, not latency config). HONEST SCOPE NOTE (important, do not overclaim): this is NOT a reimplementation of Average Lagging / LAAL / YAAL -- those are token-level, source-consumption-position formulas that need per-target-token source-alignment data this pipeline's event log does not carry at that granularity. This is a simpler join of metrics already computed elsewhere in this repo, which is enough to answer the human's direct question ('what happened to the real-time-benchmark-beyond-chrF investigation') honestly: CLA (ASR word latency) and NE (flicker) were both operationalized into code in prior cycles; a genuine unified AL/LAAL/YAAL-style single joint metric has NOT been implemented and would need new per-target-token timestamp instrumentation in the live pipeline (a bigger, code-touching hypothesis, not a retroactive analysis) -- flagged to the human as the concrete next step if a single joint number (not just a joined table) is wanted. CONCRETE RECOMMENDATION for next cycle if pursued: instrument llm_translator.py's translate_stream to timestamp each streamed target chunk against the source words consumed so far (available in _build_user_prompt's growing source text), which would allow computing real per-utterance AL directly rather than approximating it via this join.

hypotheses.title: Feasibility check: Gemini Live API native speech-to-speech translation as a Deepgram+text-LLM cascade replacement
hypotheses.description: This repo's dominant latency cost (per h-asr-final-emission-latency, h-cla-asr-latency-metric) is ASR-side: Deepgram endpointing/soft-finalize wait before translation even starts, not the LLM translation call itself (confirmed again this cycle by h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition: LLM stream time is ~0.04s mean). Gemini's gemini-3.5-live-translate-preview model does end-to-end audio-to-audio live speech translation across 70+ languages in a single WebSocket session, potentially eliminating the separate ASR-finalization-then-MT-call cascade structure entirely. $0 feasibility check (no live API calls needed): read the official docs to determine whether this could realistically replace this repo's Deepgram+Gemini-text cascade for its actual use case (live TEXT captions for Zoom/YouTube, not audio playback).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expected to find real integration barriers (following the same pattern as h-deepgram-flux-eot-availability-check's Deepgram Flux finding: technically interesting, but a bigger architecture change than a per-cycle hypothesis can safely gate).
hypotheses.required_changes: None yet -- pure research/documentation this cycle. If pursued: a new experiment-only pipeline variant piping raw audio directly to the Gemini Live WebSocket instead of Deepgram, discarding or repurposing the mandatory synthesized audio output, and using the API's optional text-transcription side channel as the caption source.
hypotheses.result_summary: $0 feasibility check via WebFetch on ai.google.dev (succeeded directly in this session -- see papers.json gemini-live-api-2026-translate-doc). CONCLUSION: not a drop-in replacement. Two hard blockers for this repo's actual use case: (1) 'Text input is not supported' -- audio-only input, so this would replace Deepgram entirely (not just the MT stage), a much bigger architecture change than the hypothesis's initial framing assumed; (2) 'Text-only output mode is unavailable; audio generation is mandatory' -- this repo's product is live TEXT captions, so using this model means paying for and generating synthesized target-language audio just to extract its optional text-transcription side channel for captions, an awkward and costly fit. No latency numbers are given in the docs themselves, and this cycle's separate search for third-party numbers found conflicting figures (300ms-2.3s Google-reported general range vs. ~3s in some independent measurements for a similarly-named model) that were not verified against this specific translate-preview model -- so even the core premise (this would actually be faster end-to-end than the current Deepgram+text-LLM cascade) is unverified, not just the integration cost. RECOMMENDATION (same pattern as the Deepgram Flux finding): flag to the human as a deliberate, human-scoped architecture-exploration project (would need a real side-by-side latency/quality prototype, not a same-clip config A/B) rather than continuing as a per-cycle research-agent hypothesis. Marking tested (feasibility answered), not abandoned -- the underlying idea (single-model audio-to-audio to skip the cascade) remains plausible, just out of this pipeline's current scope.

hypotheses.title: Raise (or disable) the fixed deepgram_max_interim_duration soft-finalize timer
hypotheses.description: h-asr-final-emission-latency (cycle 11) already proved, via static analysis of real experiment data, that config.py's deepgram_max_interim_duration=2.5s constant -- NOT the swept deepgram_endpointing value (300-2000ms) -- is what cuts roughly half to two-thirds of all translation-triggering batches, completely decoupled from the endpointing sweep. That hypothesis's own flagged next step (never executed, blocked at the time on this sandbox's Deepgram WS access) was: rerun the endpointing sweep with deepgram_max_interim_duration raised well above 2.5s (or set to None/disabled) so Deepgram's own endpointing-driven finalize actually governs most commits, and see whether end-to-end/CLA latency and cross-batch flicker (NE) move as a result. This is a config-only change (DEEPGRAM_MAX_INTERIM_DURATION env var, no code edit) on the same cached clip already used by the chunk_latency_sweep family.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Raising the timer should let genuine Deepgram-endpointing-driven finalizes (is_utterance_end=True via real silence detection, not the timer) become the majority of commits; if h-endpointing-connection-verify's explanation (a) is right (this clip's pauses just don't fall in the 300-2000ms sweep range), overall commit latency may increase slightly (waiting longer for real silence) but cross-batch flicker (translation_ne_char_cross_batch_mean, currently ~0.84 in the best config per h-masking-holdback-rpm-matched-retest's baseline) should drop, since fewer utterances get mid-timer-cut into artificial continuation batches (h-utterance-batch-timing already showed most multi-batch spans cross into a second batch almost exactly at the 2.5s timer).
hypotheses.required_changes: No code change. Set DEEPGRAM_MAX_INTERIM_DURATION to e.g. 5.0/8.0/None via env var when invoking real-time-translation-exp-youtube on the same wjZofJX0v4M 300-390s clip/window and rpm-unlimited setting the current_best_demo baseline used, so it is a clean single-variable A/B against that baseline.
experiment_ids: experiments/20260916_h_max_interim_6s_test.json (v1, DISCARDED: accidental reading_speed_chars_per_sec confound, see result_summary)
experiments/20260916_h_max_interim_6s_test_v2.json (v2, clean single-variable run used for the result below)
hypotheses.result_summary: rm-2278 explicitly authorized using .env's live Deepgram/Gemini keys for this session (previously withheld pending approval). Ran a clean single-variable A/B against the current_best_demo baseline (deepgram_max_interim_duration=2.5) on the same cached clip (wjZofJX0v4M 300-390s), same --endpointing 300, gemini_rpm_limit=60 (from .env), reading_speed_budget_translation=1 + reading_speed_chars_per_sec=4.5 pinned explicitly. FIRST ATTEMPT (h_max_interim_6s_test.json) had a real confound caught by the standard config-diff check: reading_speed_chars_per_sec came out at the code default 6.0 instead of baseline's 4.5 (not pinned via env var), so it was discarded and rerun as v2 with that variable explicitly pinned -- config diff for v2 confirmed exactly ONE difference (deepgram_max_interim_duration: 2.5 -> 6.0). RESULT (v2, clean): avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds 6.408s -> 6.182s (~4% better), max_end_to_end_latency_seconds 9.26s -> 6.59s (~29% better, meaningfully tighter tail), avg_mt_latency_seconds 1.400s -> 0.177s (~87% lower). Mechanism, confirmed via flicker_metrics.py: num_multi_batch_spans (utterances forced to split across >=2 translation batches by the timer) dropped from 15 (baseline) to just 1 (treatment) out of ~21 utterances -- i.e. raising the timer from 2.5s to 6s let nearly every utterance complete in a single translation batch instead of being cut mid-utterance and re-translated as a continuation, exactly the mechanism h-asr-final-emission-latency predicted. asr_ne_word_mean and num_asr_utterance_groups (21) were IDENTICAL between baseline and treatment (Deepgram's own transcription of the same audio bytes is deterministic and unaffected by this timer, as expected -- deepgram_endpointing, not deepgram_max_interim_duration, governs ASR-level utterance boundaries). CAVEAT (stated plainly, not smoothed over): translation_ne_char_cross_batch_mean (flicker) came out WORSE in the raw number (0.959 -> 3.0), but this is from a single multi-batch span in the treatment run vs. 15 in baseline -- not a statistically meaningful sample, and mechanically expected: with almost no multi-batch spans left to measure, the one that remains is not representative. The more meaningful read is that flicker exposure (the number of utterances even AT RISK of cross-batch rewriting) dropped by ~93% (15->1), which is a bigger and more reliable win than a single-span NE value can show. full_asr/full_translation text length differed between the two live runs (958->1507 chars ASR, 402->493 chars translation) despite supposedly identical audio -- live Deepgram WS runs over real network timing are not perfectly reproducible run-to-run in how much of the tail gets captured within the fixed wall-clock window, a known limitation of these live (not replayed) experiments; not fully investigated further here, flagged for anyone comparing full-text-length-derived metrics (e.g. chrF coverage) across separate live runs of the 'same' clip. CONCLUSION: prediction CONFIRMED on the primary metrics (latency down, especially the tail; multi-batch fragmentation down ~93%). Recommend raising the production default deepgram_max_interim_duration from 2.5s -- worth testing one or two more values (e.g. 8-10s, or disabled) to find where returns diminish, and re-running with a reference translation for a real chrF comparison before calling this final.

hypotheses.title: Cheap LLM completeness-classifier call to gate early commit vs. hold, instead of a fixed timer/silence threshold
hypotheses.description: Three independent 2026 papers found this cycle (fastturn2026-turn-detection, phoenix-vad2026-semantic-endpoint, simulsense2026-sense-driven-interpreting) converge on the same critique this repo already validated empirically (h-endpointing-pause-vs-sentence-boundary-audit: 85-94% of committed utterance-ends land mid-sentence at every endpointing threshold tested): silence-duration-only endpointing is structurally the wrong signal, because natural speech pauses mid-thought at least as often as it pauses at real turn boundaries. All three papers' actual fix is a separately-trained model (SUD/turn-detector), not implementable here without local training infra. But the underlying decision -- 'does the text so far look like a complete clause, or will it obviously continue' -- is exactly the kind of thing a fast, cheap LLM API call can answer zero-shot with a short structured-output prompt, no fine-tuning needed. Add an optional gating step: on each growing ASR interim, before the existing timer/endpointing-driven soft-finalize logic fires, make one small/cheap classifier call (a separate lightweight prompt, not the main translation call) asking whether the text-so-far is a complete clause; use a confident 'yes' to commit EARLIER than the current 2.5s timer would, and a confident 'no' near the timer boundary to extend the hold briefly rather than cutting mid-word.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Should reduce both the mid-sentence commit rate (h-endpointing-pause-vs-sentence-boundary-audit's finding) and cross-batch flicker (translation_ne_char_cross_batch_mean), similar in spirit to h-masking-holdback-rpm-matched-retest's ~28% NE reduction but via a different mechanism (deciding WHEN to commit, not truncating WHAT is sent); some added latency per classifier call, but h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition (this cycle) shows LLM response time itself is cheap (~0.04s mean) so a small classification call should be much faster than the ASR-side wait it could help avoid.
hypotheses.required_changes: New gating hook in deepgram_client.py/pipeline.py's soft-finalize path (near _maybe_commit_local_agreement, per h-localagreement-asr-commit's existing precedent for a commit-decision hook) calling llm_translator.py's LLM client with a short, separate, cheap completeness-check prompt; gated behind a new Config flag (e.g. SEMANTIC_COMPLETENESS_GATING_ENABLED) so it is opt-in and does not touch the default production path. IMPORTANT per PLAYBOOK.md's GENERATE_HYPOTHESES note: before implementing, verify which TimedEvent kind/field this hook would actually read from (is_utterance_end vs is_final semantics already tripped up three prior hypotheses) against the real construction sites in deepgram_client.py, not assumed.
experiment_ids: experiments/20260917_h_semantic_gating_test_v2.json (v2, after routing classifier calls through the rate limiter)
hypotheses.result_summary:
Implemented (LLMTranslator.check_completeness -- a minimal, separate, non-translation classifier call -- wired into DeepgramTranscriber's existing periodic force-finalize loop, debounced by semantic_gating_check_interval; see implementation commit). Verified the gating mechanism itself with 2 standalone async tests (bypassing the network, no API spend) before running live: a True-returning classifier correctly fires an early soft-finalize past semantic_gating_min_elapsed, a False-returning one never fires early and is correctly debounced. Then ran 1 live A/B against h_max_interim_6s_test_v2; config diff confirmed clean (only the 3 new fields differ). RESULT: mixed -- the mechanism demonstrably worked as designed, but overall latency got worse, likely for an architectural reason found during analysis, not because the underlying idea is wrong. The one multi-batch span in this run settled its first batch at 3.08s (vs the 6.0s timer it would otherwise have waited for) -- direct evidence the semantic gate fired early -- and that span's cross-batch NE was a PERFECT 0.0 (vs baseline's single-span NE of 3.0), i.e. the classifier correctly judged the interim complete enough that no later revision was needed at all. Coverage was fine (full_asr_len 1507 -> 1568 chars, no LocalAgreement-style collapse) and structure was similar to baseline (1/21 multi-batch spans in both). BUT aggregate latency got worse: avg_end_to_end +2.7% (6.182s -> 6.350s), max_end_to_end +40% (6.589s -> 9.207s), avg_mt_latency +21% (0.177s -> 0.215s). LIKELY CAUSE (not fully confirmed, flagged as an implementation gap rather than proof the idea fails): check_completeness's classifier calls do NOT go through self._translation_rate_limiter.acquire() the way the main translation calls in pipeline.py's _translation_worker do -- they are unthrottled extra Gemini API calls competing for the same provider-side capacity as the real translation calls, which could plausibly explain the latency cost outweighing the one confirmed benefit on this run. Also not logged as its own event kind, so classifier-call frequency/ cost is currently invisible to this repo's own analysis tooling (mt_latency_decomposition.py etc. can't see it). CONCLUSION: not adopting as-is, but NOT rejecting the underlying idea either -- this is the first hypothesis this session where the confirmed mechanism (early, correct commit) produced a genuinely better quality outcome (NE 3.0 -> 0.0 on the one observable case), unlike LocalAgreement/confidence-gating's clear failures. RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP if pursued further: route check_completeness calls through the same rate limiter as translation calls (or a separate, smaller one) before re-testing, and log classifier calls as their own event kind so their cost/frequency is measurable.

UPDATE (same session, after fixing the rate-limiter gap): routed check_completeness through the same RateLimiter the translation workers use (moved its construction earlier in TranslationPipeline.__init__, wrapped the classifier callback with an acquire() gate before calling it; verified wiring with a mocked pipeline construction before spending API budget). Reran the live A/B (h_semantic_gating_test_v2). RESULT: the fix worked -- max_end_to_end_latency_seconds dropped from v1's 9.207s (+40% vs baseline) to 6.789s (+3.0% vs baseline's 6.589s), eliminating the bad outlier. avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds +3.1% (6.182s -> 6.372s, about the same as v1's +2.7%), avg_mt_latency_seconds +30% (0.177s -> 0.230s, still elevated but the worst symptom is gone). Coverage fine (full_asr_len 1507 -> 1474, within normal run-to-run variance). This run had 2 multi-batch spans (vs baseline's 1): one settled early at 3.12s (semantic gate fired) with NE=0.6 -- notably better than baseline's typical single-span NE of ~3.0 -- the other settled at the full 6.82s timer (gate never fired confidently for it) with NE=3.0, matching baseline. Weighted cross-batch NE for this run: 1.8, vs baseline's 3.0. CONCLUSION (revised): after the rate-limiter fix, this hypothesis shows a modest, genuine, DOUBLE-SIDED signal -- some latency cost remains (avg_mt +30%) but quality improves where the gate engages (NE roughly halved on the cases it caught). Still not a clear-cut production recommendation on a single 90s run each side, but meaningfully more promising than any of the other 2 literature-grounded hypotheses tested this session (both of which showed no benefit at all or clear harm). Worth a longer/repeated test before a final call, and worth checking whether semantic_gating_min_elapsed/check_interval tuning can reduce the residual avg_mt cost further.

hypotheses.title: Prompt-level source-word-order-preserving (monotonic) translation for EN->JA interim commits
hypotheses.description: makinae2024-word-order-sync-metric (found this cycle) argues that for distant-word-order pairs like English-Japanese, real simultaneous interpreters deliberately preserve source word order (at some cost to natural Japanese phrasing) specifically because it reduces how much of the sentence they need to hear before they can start producing correct output -- Japanese's verb-final/SOV structure otherwise forces waiting for clause-final material. This repo's current translation prompt (llm_translator.py's system prompt / _build_user_prompt) has never been tested for an explicit monotonic/chunk-wise-order instruction; the existing masking-holdback and continuation-anchor hypotheses changed WHEN/WHAT text is sent, not the requested translation STYLE. Add an opt-in prompt variant instructing the LLM to prefer source-order-preserving Japanese phrasing (accepting reduced naturalness) specifically for non-utterance-final (interim/continuation) batches, falling back to natural phrasing once is_utterance_end=True allows a final, fluent rewrite.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: If the word-order-mismatch theory is right, monotonic-style interim translations should require less lookahead to produce a plausible partial rendering, which should show up as lower cross-batch flicker (less need to revise word order as more source arrives) and/or lower effective per-batch latency (less waiting for enough source context before committing to a translation), at some cost to chrF/naturalness on the interim text specifically (final utterance-end text should be minimally affected since it still gets the natural-phrasing fallback).
hypotheses.required_changes: New prompt template variant in llm_translator.py's _get_system_prompt/_build_user_prompt, gated behind a new Config flag (e.g. MONOTONIC_INTERIM_TRANSLATION_ENABLED), applied only when the batch is not utterance-final. A/B against the current_best_demo baseline on the same clip/window.
hypotheses.result_summary: Implemented (Config.monotonic_interim_translation_enabled, threaded through translate_stream/_build_user_prompt and pipeline.py's _translation_worker, gated on `not is_last_of_utterance` -- see implementation commit). Ran 1 live A/B against the h_max_interim_6s_test_v2 baseline; config diff confirmed exactly 1 difference. RESULT: essentially a wash on aggregate metrics -- avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds 6.182s -> 6.301s (+1.9%), max_end_to_end_latency_seconds 6.589s -> 6.729s (+2.1%), avg_mt_latency_seconds 0.177s -> 0.187s (+5.6%), all small enough to plausibly be live-run noise. Coverage identical (full_asr_len 1507 chars both). Cross-batch NE on the single multi-batch span got slightly worse (3.0 -> 3.27, n=1). METHODOLOGICAL FINDING (the important part): this hypothesis's instruction only ever applies to a NOT-YET-utterance-final batch (`not is_last_of_utterance`), and this clip -- now that h-max-interim-duration-raise consolidated batching -- has only 1 multi-batch span out of 21 utterances, meaning the monotonic instruction was only actually injected into 2 translation calls total (both runs). Manually inspected those exact 2 calls: baseline '次に、そのAIアシスタントがどう返答するかを予測させます。さらに、' vs monotonic 'そして、その有能なAIアシスタントがどう答えるかを予測させます。さらに、' -- minor lexical differences, no visible word-order restructuring either way, consistent with the source content at that point already being fairly monotonic-friendly (simple SVO-adjacent clauses) rather than a case that would stress-test the hypothesis. CONCLUSION: NOT a meaningful test of the underlying idea -- this is now the THIRD hypothesis in a row (after h-masking-holdback-x-raised-timer and h-continuation-anchor-x-raised-timer) to hit the exact same structural ceiling: any technique that only acts on continuation batches has almost nothing to act on now that the timer raise collapsed most utterances to a single batch. RECOMMENDATION: do not conclude anything about the monotonic-phrasing idea itself from this run. A fair test needs either a clip with genuinely long/continuous utterances that still cross multiple 6s batches even at the raised timer (this clip's utterances are mostly short), or a different test design entirely (e.g. directly comparing monotonic vs natural phrasing on ALREADY-known-long source text, not gated by batch position).

hypotheses.title: 2x2 factorial: soft-final interval (2.5s vs ~4s) x continuation strategy (retranslate-from-scratch vs append-continue)
hypotheses.description: Human-proposed (rm-2278, 2026-09-16, while reviewing the soft-finalize flow diagram). Two currently-separate, independently-motivated changes should be tested together as a 2x2 grid rather than one at a time: (1) Config.deepgram_max_interim_duration, currently fixed at 2.5s -- h-max-interim-duration-raise (queued, needs_human, never run) already argues for raising this to ~4-5s on the grounds that h-utterance-batch-timing showed most multi-batch spans cross into a second batch almost exactly at the 2.5s mark, i.e. the timer itself (not real speech pauses) is the dominant cause of batch-splitting. (2) The continuation-batch translation strategy: today, ANY continuation batch (is_utterance_end=False) re-translates the ENTIRE accumulated source text from scratch every time (pipeline.py _stream_batch, full_target_text), a deliberate design choice per the code's own comment (pipeline.py:216-225) that gluing independently-translated fragments produces grammatically incoherent output. h-continuation-context-anchor (tested, cycle 9-13) already tried a lighter variant of relaxing this -- passing the utterance's own prior translation as an extra <prior_translation> anchor block while STILL feeding and re-translating the full accumulated source -- and found no clear improvement (translation_ne_char_cross_batch_mean 0.972 vs baseline 0.836, i.e. slightly worse, though confounded by run-to-run batching variance the same experiment surfaced). This hypothesis proposes going further: a genuine append-continue mode where, for continuation batches only, the translator is given a DEDICATED continuation prompt (distinct from the existing verbatim-translation system prompt used for is_utterance_end=True final commits) containing only the NEW source delta since the last commit (new_text, not full_target_text) plus the prior_translation already shown on screen, and instructed to produce ONLY the text to append -- not to restate or re-derive the earlier part. The true is_utterance_end=True commit still gets a full pass (either the existing from-scratch retranslation of the whole utterance, or a lighter cleanup pass over the concatenated append output -- pick whichever is cheaper to implement first and note the choice in the writeup) so any accumulated incoherence from the append steps gets one chance to be smoothed at the point the utterance is known to be complete. Crossing this 2x2 with the interval change matters because they interact: a longer soft-final interval means fewer, larger continuation events, so any per-continuation coherence risk from append-mode fires less often, while a shorter interval means append-mode's coherence risk (if any) compounds more times per utterance -- neither axis alone tells you whether append-mode is safe to combine with the interval fix h-max-interim-duration-raise already recommends.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expect the 4 cells to rank roughly: (2.5s, retranslate) = today's baseline, highest cross-batch NE (~0.84-1.47 per h-cross-utterance-flicker/h-masking-holdback-rpm-matched-retest's baselines) but presumed-safest coherence; (4s, retranslate) should reduce NE mainly by reducing the NUMBER of multi-batch utterances (h-utterance-batch-timing's mechanism), independent of any translation-strategy change; (2.5s, append) tests whether append-mode alone helps NE despite firing often, at highest risk of the glued-fragment incoherence pipeline.py's own design comment warns about; (4s, append) tests whether the two fixes compound (fewer, and individually lower-NE, continuations) or whether append-mode's coherence risk dominates regardless of interval. A result where append-mode reduces NE but chrF/fidelity-judge score drops would replicate the same fidelity-vs-compression-style tradeoff h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction and Config.reading_speed_budget_translation (commits 33faed4/c4fd798) already found for other prompt-side interventions -- so fidelity/coherence must be scored alongside NE for all 4 cells, not NE alone.
hypotheses.required_changes: config.py: no change needed for the interval axis (DEEPGRAM_MAX_INTERIM_DURATION env var already supported, per h-max-interim-duration-raise). Add a new Config flag (e.g. continuation_translation_mode: Literal['retranslate','append'] = 'retranslate') for the strategy axis. llm_translator.py: add a distinct continuation-only prompt path (system + user template) used only when mode='append' and is_continuation, reusing the prior_translation plumbing h-continuation-context-anchor already added (self._utterance_translated_text) but feeding new_text instead of full_target_text as the source block. pipeline.py _stream_batch: branch text_to_translate/prompt selection on the new Config flag; keep is_utterance_end=True path using the existing full-retranslation call unconditionally (or add a documented lighter alternative) regardless of mode, so there is always one full-utterance quality pass at commit time. Run all 4 cells on the same cached clip/window used by current_best_demo (commit 3b31e18) for a clean single-clip comparison; score each with flicker_metrics.py's group_translation_by_utterance (cross-batch NE) plus chrF and a fidelity-judge pass (reuse the holistic judge mechanism h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction used) so a coherence regression is caught even if NE improves. NOTE: like h-max-interim-duration-raise and h-continuation-context-anchor before it, testing the append-mode axis needs a REAL live Deepgram-driven run (continuation batches only exist with live streaming input, not retroactive replay of already-saved JSON) -- check current Deepgram listen-websocket access before starting; this has been blocked by a proxy WS-upgrade-mangling issue in the sandboxed cloud environment across cycles 5-15 (unblocked, per prior cycles, only when rm-2278 runs it locally).
hypotheses.result_summary: SCOPING DECISION (documented, see implementation commit): tested the mode axis alone at the OLD 2.5s timer (where continuation batches are common, ~15/21 utterances per current_best_demo's own data) rather than the full 2x2 factorial the hypothesis originally proposed -- the interval axis is already separately validated (h-max-interim-duration-raise), and this session's re-tests of 3 other continuation-only techniques at the 6.0s production timer all hit the same wall: only 1/21 utterances is a multi-batch span there, too few to evaluate any continuation-targeted technique meaningfully. Reused current_best_demo (2.5s timer, retranslate mode, same clip/window/rpm) as the control instead of rerunning it, and ran ONE new live experiment (continuation_translation_mode=append). Config diff: only continuation_translation_mode differs (the other 'diffs' shown are schema-version artifacts -- fields added to the config dump after current_best_demo was recorded, all effectively 'off' in both runs). ASR was bit-identical (full_asr_len 958 chars both, segment_count 16 both) -- a very clean comparison. RESULT: genuinely positive, and unlike every other technique retested this session, STATISTICALLY WELL-POWERED (15 multi-batch spans each side, not n=1). translation_ne_char_cross_batch_mean: 0.959 (control) -> 0.715 (append), a ~25% reduction -- comparable in magnitude to masking-holdback's own best result (~28% under the old timer) but via a fundamentally different, more principled mechanism (changing HOW continuations are translated, not truncating what's sent). Latency cost was minimal, unlike holdback's real wall-clock-draining cost: avg_end_to_end_latency +0.5% (6.408s -> 6.440s), max_end_to_end +7.2% (9.26s -> 9.926s), avg_mt_latency +7.3% (1.4s -> 1.502s). Manually inspected a representative multi-batch span's actual text (per the hypothesis's own required coherence check): batch 1 (continuation, append mode) = 'これはあくまで概要ですが、その後、プロセスは', batch 2 (is_utterance_end=True, full retranslation pass) = 'これはあくまで概要ですが、その後、プロセスは基本的に繰り返され、戻って' -- the continuation text is an EXACT, coherent prefix of the final text, confirming append mode is not producing the 'glued incoherent fragments' pipeline.py's own original design comment warned about, at least on this evidence. CONCLUSION: the single most promising result of any hypothesis tested this session -- a real, well-powered flicker reduction at a small, bounded latency cost, with manually-confirmed coherent output. RECOMMENDATION: worth enabling alongside the validated 6.0s timer in the production/best-known config -- the mechanism has no inherent duration-dependent downside (unlike holdback's queue-draining cost under rate limits), so there is little risk in having it available for the rare continuation case even though most utterances won't exercise it at 6.0s. A formal combined (6.0s + append) A/B would still suffer the same n=1 sample-size problem as the other continuation-only retests, so this recommendation rests on the 2.5s result generalizing, not on a direct 6.0s-timer test -- flagged as the one open caveat.

hypotheses.title: Scale translation compression aggressiveness to live translation-queue backlog depth, not just this utterance's own speech duration
hypotheses.description: Human-proposed (rm-2278, 2026-09-16, while reviewing the soft-finalize flow diagram): the diagram's timeline made visible that some on-screen caption fragments represent only a fraction of a second of speech (e.g. a soft-final that lands moments after the previous one), which are effectively unreadable regardless of translation quality -- not because any single utterance is too information-dense, but because the SYSTEM is behind. Config.reading_speed_budget_translation (commits 33faed4/c4fd798, landed 2026-09-15) already derives a target character budget from speech_duration, but that duration is computed purely from THIS utterance's own start/end timestamps (pipeline.py _stream_batch: speech_start to batch[-1].end_time) -- it has no visibility into the shared translation queue's actual backlog (the _FragmentQueue behind translation_queue_size=20, drained by translation_workers=4 concurrent workers) or the queue-wait component h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition (tested, this cycle) already isolated as a distinct latency term from LLM-stream-duration. Two utterances with identical own-speech-duration can therefore get identical compression treatment today even if one is translated while the queue is empty and the other while 15 fragments are backed up -- the second is exactly the case producing back-to-back, barely-readable fragments, and per-utterance duration alone cannot see that. Proposal: add a second, backlog-derived signal to the existing reading-speed-budget mechanism (or the compression-actions prompt from h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction) -- e.g. current queue depth (len of the pending items in _FragmentQueue) or the measured queue-wait time for the batch about to be translated -- and tighten the character budget (or escalate to more aggressive SENTENCE_CUT/DROP-style instructions) when backlog is high, on the theory that compressing harder while behind lets the pipeline spend fewer output characters per unit of wall-clock catch-up time, amortizing the latency debt across denser captions instead of emitting a rapid sequence of near-instantaneous, unreadable fragments.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expect the fraction of on-screen fragments below some minimum-readable-duration threshold (needs a new metric -- does not exist yet, would need to be computed from batch[-1].end_time - batch[0].start_time and each event's own emit timestamp, similar in spirit to h-cla-asr-latency-metric's approach) to drop under high-backlog conditions relative to the current fixed per-utterance budget, at some chrF/fidelity cost concentrated specifically in the high-backlog batches (per h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction and reading_speed_budget_translation's own findings that compression instructions carry a real, not-fully-guardrailable content-fidelity risk -- this hypothesis should expect and measure the same risk, not assume it away because the trigger condition is different).
hypotheses.required_changes: First define the missing 'unreadable fragment' metric itself (e.g. in flicker_metrics.py or a new module) before touching production code, since PLAYBOOK.md's own policy is not to claim an effect without first being able to measure the thing the hypothesis is about. pipeline.py: expose queue depth (self._transcription_queue.qsize() or equivalent) or per-batch queue-wait (h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition already computes something like this) to the _stream_batch call site; extend the reading_speed_budget_translation calculation (or add a new backlog_adaptive_compression Config flag, kept separate so it can be A/B'd independently of the existing per-utterance-duration budget) to fold in a backlog term. Needs a live run with genuinely variable backlog (e.g. a clip with a fast, dense speech passage to induce real queue buildup) rather than retroactive replay, since backlog is a property of live concurrent worker timing, not something recoverable from already-saved experiment JSON alone -- same Deepgram listen-websocket access caveat as the other queued/proposed hypotheses in this backlog.
experiment_ids: experiments/20260917_h_backlog_compression_control.json (rpm=60, LLM2025 guest talk clip, denser/faster speech)
experiments/20260918_h_backlog_compression_control_rpm9.json (rpm=9, same clip, deliberately constrained to try to induce backlog)
hypotheses.result_summary: First defined the missing 'unreadable fragment' metric retroactively by composing two EXISTING tools this repo already had (subtitle_formatter.extract_utterance_cues/format_naive for real wall-clock cue timing via _clip_to_next_start, readability_metrics.analyze_readability for CPS/duration violations against Netflix/BBC standards) -- no new metric logic needed, just a glue script (caption_readability_from_experiment.py). Ran it over the full 90-experiment corpus: confirmed the premise is real in principle -- llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min (the known rpm=9-throttled run from before this session) shows a 41.5% caption duration-violation rate. Then implemented Config.backlog_adaptive_compression_enabled (scales reading_speed_budget_translation's character budget down by up to 50% as len(_transcription_queue) approaches translation_queue_size); verified the scaling formula's correctness with a pure unit-level check (queue_depth 0/2/5/8/10/15 against queue_size=10 produces target_chars 20/18/15/12/10/10 for a base budget of 20 -- linear scaling down to 50% at full queue, capped, exactly as designed) before any live spend. LIVE TESTING: ran a denser/faster-paced clip (LLM2025 guest talk, the same source that showed real backlog under the old rpm=9-era config) at the validated 6.0s timer -- FIRST at rpm=60 (avg_mt_latency 0.151s, no sign of backlog), THEN deliberately at rpm=9 specifically to try to force backlog (avg_mt_latency actually LOWER at 0.109s, still no backlog). CONCLUSION: could not observe real backlog forming on this clip even under a deliberately constrained rpm=9 -- the flag has nothing to act on in either run (backlog_ratio stays ~0 throughout), so no live A/B differential is possible without a harder stress test. ROOT CAUSE (a 4th instance of the same underlying pattern this session): h-max-interim-duration-raise's fix (fewer, larger translation batches) also drastically cuts total translation-call FREQUENCY, which incidentally starves the backlog problem of its original trigger too -- the historical 41.5%-violation-rate run was recorded under the OLD 2.5s timer (many more, smaller, more frequent calls), not the now-validated 6.0s one. NOT rejecting the underlying idea -- the mechanism is implemented and verified correct -- but flagging that, like 3 other continuation/frequency-targeted hypotheses this session, its premise's original trigger condition (frequent small translation calls) has been substantially resolved by the timer fix already recommended for production. Would need either a much harder stress test (e.g. rpm=2-3, or a genuinely faster-spoken source) or a live run long/eventful enough to hit a real network/provider hiccup to observe this flag actually engaging.

hypotheses.title: Gate early soft-finalize on Deepgram's own per-word confidence, not just the fixed timer
hypotheses.description: h-max-interim-duration-raise (this session, live A/B) confirmed raising the fixed 2.5s soft-finalize timer to 6.0s cuts mid-utterance splits from 15/21 to 1/21 utterances and lowers max end-to-end latency ~29% -- but a fixed timer, longer or not, is still a blind proxy for 'has enough evidence arrived to commit'. x2streaming-asr2026 (found this session) frames streaming ASR as exactly this question (when to commit vs what to commit) and industry practice (found via a separate search) already gates partial-translation emission on ASR confidence exceeding ~0.7, retranslating only if the committed prefix later changes. This repo ALREADY logs a `confidence` field on every asr_interim event (deepgram_client.py's TranscriptionResult, confidence < 0.7 already flagged via the existing `is_low_confidence` property, currently only used to annotate displayed text with '[uncertain: ...]' in pipeline.py:393, not to gate commit timing) -- so this needs zero new API calls, just a new decision rule using data already flowing through the pipeline. Add an optional early-commit path: if a growing interim's confidence stays above a threshold (e.g. 0.85-0.9) for its own is_utterance_end-eligible span, allow a soft-finalize before the fixed max_interim_duration timer fires; if confidence drops, fall back to the existing timer/endpointing behavior unchanged.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Should further reduce average commit latency beyond what h-max-interim-duration-raise alone achieves (committing confidently-correct speech sooner than a fixed 6s wait), without the cost or added round-trip of h-semantic-completeness-gating's extra LLM call, since it reuses data already collected. Risk: high ASR confidence does not equal semantically-complete (a confidently-transcribed word can still be mid-clause), so this may need to be combined with, not substituted for, a semantic check -- worth testing standalone first to isolate its own effect.
hypotheses.required_changes: New confidence-based early-commit branch in deepgram_client.py's soft-finalize path (same area as h-localagreement-asr-commit's _maybe_commit_local_agreement precedent), reading the already-populated `confidence` field, gated behind a new Config flag (e.g. ASR_CONFIDENCE_EARLY_COMMIT_THRESHOLD, None = disabled). Per PLAYBOOK.md's GENERATE_HYPOTHESES note, verify exactly which event kind(s) carry a populated `confidence` at the point this hook would read it (asr_interim per the grep in this entry's grounding, not assumed for other kinds) before implementing.
hypotheses.result_summary: Implemented (Config.asr_confidence_early_commit_threshold/_min_elapsed, wired through DeepgramTranscriber._force_finalize_loop's existing 0.5s periodic check -- see the implementation commit). Ran 2 live A/Bs against the h_max_interim_6s_test_v2 baseline (deepgram_max_interim_duration=6.0, rpm=60), varying only min_elapsed. PRE-CHECK finding that shaped both runs: this clip's confidence distribution is highly concentrated near 1.0 (91 asr_interim samples: median=0.999, p10=0.996, only a few outliers down to 0.82) -- confidence>=0.99 is satisfied almost immediately for nearly every interim on this clip. V1 (min_elapsed=3.0s): config diff confirmed clean (only the 2 new fields differ). RESULT: WORSE across the board, resembling LocalAgreement-2's failure mode. num_multi_batch_spans jumped from baseline's 1/21 to 11/14 (early-commit fired near the 3.0s floor almost every time, since confidence is essentially always satisfied), first_batch_duration_mean dropped 6.82s -> 3.93s (undoing most of h-max-interim-duration-raise's benefit). avg_mt_latency_seconds 0.177s -> 1.006s (~5.7x worse), avg_end_to_end +6%, max_end_to_end +14%. Coverage also collapsed: full_asr_len 1507 -> 863 chars (~43% less content processed in the same wall-clock window), full_translation_len 493 -> 315 chars -- the SAME coverage-collapse signature LocalAgreement-2 showed both times it was tested, now seen here too. Root cause: with confidence saturated near 1.0, the gate doesn't meaningfully discriminate -- it degenerates into 'soft-finalize every min_elapsed seconds regardless of confidence,' i.e. effectively just a much lower timer (3.0s instead of 6.0s), which is already known to be worse (this is exactly what h-max-interim-duration-raise showed by going the OTHER direction, 2.5s -> 6.0s). V2 (min_elapsed=5.0s, narrower window closer to the 6.0s ceiling): avoided v1's fragmentation and coverage collapse -- num_multi_batch_spans back to 1/21 (matching baseline's structure), full_asr_len 1507 -> 1594 (no coverage loss, if anything slightly more captured), cross-batch NE on the one remaining span actually improved (3.0 -> 0.83). But no clear latency win either: avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds +3.4% (6.182s -> 6.392s), max_end_to_end_latency_seconds +44% (6.589s -> 9.491s, a real outlier), avg_mt_latency +45% (0.177s -> 0.257s). Given the batching STRUCTURE is nearly identical to baseline (1 vs 1 multi-batch span), these latency differences are more plausibly live-run-to-run network/timing noise (documented before in this repo's own live-experiment caveats) than a genuine effect of the confidence gate itself, but this can't be fully disentangled with a single run per side. CONCLUSION: not adopting on this clip. The core problem is that this clip's ASR confidence isn't a useful discriminating signal (near-saturated at ~0.99-1.0 throughout) -- a noisier clip (background noise, accents, unfamiliar technical terms genuinely prone to Deepgram misrecognition) would be needed to fairly test whether confidence-gating helps when confidence actually varies meaningfully. Not abandoning the underlying idea, but flagging that THIS clip is structurally a poor testbed for it -- recommend retesting on a harder/noisier clip if pursued further, rather than tuning min_elapsed further on this one.

hypotheses.title: Feasibility check: OpenAI's gpt-realtime-translate as a Deepgram+text-LLM cascade replacement

OpenAI's gpt-realtime-translate (released 2026-05-07, found this session) is a comparable single-session audio-to-audio translation product, but its docs describe target-language transcript deltas streaming WHILE audio is still arriving (not gated behind a mandatory audio generation the way Gemini Live's docs state) -- worth its own $0 feasibility check rather than assuming the same blocker applies, especially since Japanese is confirmed in its 13-language target list (a harder requirement Gemini Live never got to, having failed on text output alone) and an independent benchmark reported a roughly constant ~3s lag (es->en/pt->en, not en->ja, so not directly comparable to this repo's own numbers without a real test).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expected to find the same class of integration barrier as Gemini Live and Deepgram Flux (bigger architecture change than a per-cycle hypothesis can gate) even if the text-output question resolves favorably, since audio-only input still means replacing Deepgram entirely, not just the MT stage.
hypotheses.required_changes: None yet -- pure research/documentation. If the text-output question resolves favorably: a new experiment-only pipeline variant piping raw audio directly to the Realtime API session instead of Deepgram, using the transcript-delta stream as the caption source.
hypotheses.result_summary: $0 feasibility check via WebSearch (developers.openai.com's realtime-translation guide page returned only partial content on direct WebFetch -- a JS-rendered docs page, not an egress block -- so this relied on search snippets and the OpenAI community forum, not primary-source page content, unlike last session's ai.google.dev check which fetched cleanly). Findings: (1) Japanese IS in the 13-language target list, clearing a bar Gemini Live never reached; (2) target-language transcript deltas stream WHILE audio is still arriving, suggesting text is closer to a first-class output than Gemini Live's phrasing implied; (3) BUT a separate search on disabling audio output found that OpenAI's general modalities:['text'] trick (which does disable audio for the plain gpt-realtime model) is documented specifically alongside a note that gpt-realtime-translate 'behaves as a dedicated interpreter' with audio input producing audio-plus-transcripts output, without confirming whether the text-only override still applies to this specialized translate mode -- genuinely unresolved from documentation alone, would need a direct API test to settle. If pursued, this is a better first candidate than Gemini Live given it clears the Japanese-language bar and appears to treat text as more central to the product design.

hypotheses.title: Does masking-holdback still help once the raised soft-finalize timer already prevents most multi-batch splits?
hypotheses.description: rm-2278 asked directly, after seeing the new captioned demo (deepgram_max_interim_duration=6.0, holdback/LocalAgreement/anchor all OFF): since holdback's ~28% cross-batch NE reduction (h-masking-holdback-rpm-matched-retest) was measured under the OLD 2.5s timer where multi-batch splits were common (15/21 utterances), and h-max-interim-duration-raise (this session) already cut that to 1/21 by raising the timer alone, does holdback still earn its latency cost once there is almost nothing left for it to fix? Live A/B: masking_holdback_words=2 on top of the validated 6.0s-timer config (h_max_interim_6s_test_v2), same clip/window/rpm, config diff confirmed exactly 1 variable changed.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: If the timer raise already addressed most of what holdback was compensating for, holdback should show little-to-no further NE benefit on this clip while still paying its known latency cost (delayed commit).
hypotheses.required_changes: None -- config-only live A/B, same as h-max-interim-duration-raise.
hypotheses.result_summary: Config diff confirmed exactly ONE difference from the h_max_interim_6s_test_v2 baseline (masking_holdback_words: 0 -> 2). RESULT: prediction CONFIRMED -- holdback has essentially nothing left to fix and pays a small net cost. Both runs produced the SAME utterance structure (21 utterances, exactly 1 multi-batch span each -- the timer raise already eliminated the other 14 that existed under the old 2.5s regime). On that one remaining multi-batch span, cross-batch NE got slightly WORSE with holdback (3.0 -> 3.4, n=1 so not individually meaningful, but directionally opposite of the predicted benefit). Latency also got slightly worse: avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds 6.182s -> 6.371s (+3%), avg_mt_latency_seconds 0.177s -> 0.184s (+4%) -- consistent with holdback's known mechanism (delaying commit by withholding trailing words) now showing up as pure cost with no offsetting flicker win, since there are almost no multi-batch continuations left for it to smooth over. ASR-side output was effectively identical (asr_ne_word_mean 0.1444 vs 0.1409, full_asr_len 1507 chars both runs -- holdback only affects the translation-side prompt, not ASR, as expected). CONCLUSION: holdback's previously-measured ~28% NE reduction (h-masking-holdback-rpm-matched-retest) does NOT carry over once the raised timer is in place -- the two fixes are NOT additive, because they target the same underlying problem (multi-batch continuation splits) from different angles, and the timer raise already solves most of it more cheaply (no per-call latency cost, no code change). RECOMMENDATION: keep masking_holdback_words=0 in the current-best config -- confirms the demo's existing choice was correct, not an oversight. Caveat: n=1 on the multi-batch-span comparison is thin; a clip with more natural long/continuous utterances (more surviving multi-batch spans even at the raised timer) would be a fairer test of whether holdback has ANY remaining value, but on this clip/config the answer is a clean no.

hypotheses.title: Does LocalAgreement-2's failure mode survive once rpm=60 (not rpm=9) is the standing config?
hypotheses.description: rm-2278 asked to re-verify all 4 rejected/adopted paper techniques from scratch against the new best-known config, discarding old conclusions. h-localagreement-asr-commit's original bad result (avg_mt_latency 61.4s, only 4/8 segments captured) was diagnosed as likely dominated by gemini_rpm_limit=9 (too many small word-level-agreement-triggered calls serializing behind a strict rate limit) -- but that diagnosis was never actually tested by removing the rpm=9 confound while keeping localagreement_commit_enabled=1. This session's .env default is now rpm=60 (rm-2278's own edit), and deepgram_max_interim_duration=6.0 is now validated -- retest localagreement_commit_enabled=1 on top of both.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: If rpm=9 was really the dominant cause, rpm=60 alone should fix most of the latency blowup. If the mechanism itself (committing on any word-level agreement fires far more, smaller calls than a natural batch boundary would) is the real problem, latency and coverage should still degrade even at rpm=60, just less catastrophically.
hypotheses.required_changes: None -- config-only live A/B, same as h-max-interim-duration-raise.
hypotheses.result_summary: Config diff confirmed exactly ONE difference from the h_max_interim_6s_test_v2 baseline (localagreement_commit_enabled: False -> True). RESULT: still clearly worse, prediction's second branch confirmed -- rpm=9 was NOT the sole cause, only a severity multiplier. avg_mt_latency_seconds 0.177s -> 3.666s (~21x worse, but nowhere near the original rpm=9 test's 61.4s -- rpm alone explains most, not all, of the original disaster's magnitude). avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds 6.182s -> 7.264s (+17%), max_end_to_end_latency_seconds 6.589s -> 9.144s (+39%). COVERAGE COLLAPSED: full_asr_len 1507 -> 839 chars (~44% less content processed in the same 90s wall-clock window) and full_translation_len 493 -> 400 chars -- this replicates the ORIGINAL h-localagreement-asr-commit finding's core failure mode (the pipeline falls behind real-time and simply processes less of the clip) even without the rpm=9 confound. Mechanism confirmed via flicker_metrics.py: num_translation_utterance_groups exploded from 22 (baseline) to 76 (localagreement) for the SAME 21 ASR utterances (asr_ne_word_mean and num_asr_utterance_groups=21 identical to baseline, confirming ASR itself is unaffected as expected) -- word-level agreement commits far more often than a natural batch boundary would, exactly as h-localagreement-asr-commit's original root-cause analysis described. num_multi_batch_spans jumped from 1/21 (baseline) to 17/21 -- the opposite direction of what raising the timer achieved for the OTHER hypotheses (fewer multi-batch splits): LocalAgreement actively RE-FRAGMENTS what the timer raise had already consolidated. CONCLUSION: rejecting LocalAgreement-2 again, but for a CORRECTED reason -- not primarily an rpm=9 rate-limit artifact (the original hypothesis's leading explanation), but a structural mismatch between word-level commit granularity and this pipeline's per-batch translation-call architecture, which persists (attenuated, not eliminated) even at a generous rpm=60. This is a genuine correction to the historical record, not just a confirmation -- worth noting in reflections.md that the original diagnosis, while reasonable given the evidence available at the time, was incomplete.

Retest anchor_continuation_translation=1 on top of the validated 6.0s timer + rpm=60 (h_max_interim_6s_test_v2 baseline), same clip/window.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Given the timer raise already cut multi-batch spans to 1/21 (same structural situation h-masking-holdback-x-raised-timer hit), expect a similarly thin, likely inconclusive result rather than a clean confirmation either way.
hypotheses.required_changes: None -- config-only live A/B.
hypotheses.result_summary: Config diff confirmed exactly ONE difference (anchor_continuation_translation: False -> True). RESULT: mixed, small effects, essentially a wash -- prediction (thin/inconclusive given rarity of multi-batch spans) confirmed. avg_mt_latency_seconds actually improved 0.177s -> 0.137s (-23%), but avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds got slightly worse 6.182s -> 6.332s (+2.4%) and max_end_to_end_latency_seconds worse 6.589s -> 7.300s (+11%).
