hypotheses.title: Decompose the guest-talk NE regression from h-soft-anchor-gate-min-words-3 into per-batch-transition erasure: is it concentrated at the gated transitions themselves, or does it propagate into later, ungated transitions of the same span? -- the focused follow-up that hypothesis's own result_summary recommended, reframed by persistent-delivery2026-revision-optimization's survives-vs-currently-visible framing
hypotheses.description: This cycle's newly-read paper (persistent-delivery2026-revision-optimization, arXiv 2609.26427) is a training-time technique for an end-to-end model and does not port to this repo's cascade, but its diagnostic framing -- distinguish content that is 'currently visible' from content that 'survives to the final revision' rather than trusting the instantaneous displayed state -- is directly applicable to the open, UNEXPLAINED finding flagged in h-soft-anchor-gate-min-words-3's result_summary (cycle 23 ANALYZE_RESULTS): on the guest-talk clip, gated_soft_anchor's mean_ne (0.377, aggregate) was markedly WORSE than soft_anchor_replay's (0.089), the opposite of the intended direction, and that result_summary explicitly recommended 'a focused follow-up hypothesis next cycle decomposing NE specifically on gated vs. non-gated batches' before drawing any conclusion. Verified directly against experiments/20260922_h_soft_anchor_gate_min3_replay.json before finalizing this hypothesis (per PLAYBOOK.md's field-verification rule), by recomputing span-level NE split on whether a span's 'gated_batch_indices' list is non-empty: on the guest-talk source, the 42 spans where the gate actually fired have gated_soft_anchor mean_ne=0.661 vs soft_anchor_replay's 0.088 (nearly as bad as the fully-ungated baseline_replay's 0.738 on the same spans), while the 41 spans where the gate never fired have gated_soft_anchor mean_ne=0.085 vs soft_anchor_replay's 0.090 -- statistically indistinguishable, exactly as expected since gated_soft_anchor and soft_anchor_replay are code-path-identical whenever nothing is gated. This confirms the coarse (span-level) version of the open question: the entire aggregate regression is concentrated in the 42 gated spans, not spread uniformly across all 125. What is NOT yet answered, and is this hypothesis's actual target, is the finer within-span question: inside those 42 gated spans, is the extra erasure attributable specifically to the transition(s) that produced a gated batch, or does holding a batch back also destabilize later, non-gated transitions in the same span (i.e. a knock-on effect, not a one-time contained re-reveal)? normalized_erasure() (flicker_metrics.py) computes NE as a sum of per-transition erasure_i = len(h_{i-1}) - lcp(h_{i-1}, h_i) over consecutive batch texts, divided by the final text's length -- so this decomposition is a direct, already-supported reframing of the existing per-span NE computation, not a new metric. Verified the exact indexing against flicker_metrics.py directly: normalized_erasure()'s internal pairwise() loop means erasure computed at loop position t (0-indexed, t=0..num_batches-2) is the erasure of the transition INTO batches[t+1], so transition t should be labeled 'gated' iff (t+1) is in that span's gated_batch_indices list -- confirmed this matches the gate's own construction (batch index i, i>0, in soft_anchor_gate_min3_replay.py) rather than assumed from the field's name alone.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Two competing, falsifiable predictions, reported honestly regardless of which one the data supports: (1) 'contained re-reveal' -- if gated_soft_anchor's excess per-transition erasure (over soft_anchor_replay, same span, same transition) is concentrated almost entirely at gated transitions themselves, with non-gated transitions in the same 42 spans showing erasure close to soft_anchor_replay's, that means the gate's cost is local and bounded to the batch it directly holds back -- a tolerable, well-understood tradeoff. (2) 'destabilization' -- if non-gated transitions within gated spans also show meaningfully elevated erasure for gated_soft_anchor relative to soft_anchor_replay, that means withholding a batch disrupts translation continuity beyond the held-back batch itself (e.g. the model re-derives a different phrasing for later content once it has finally seen the withheld span), which would be a more serious problem for this whole gating approach and should be flagged prominently in the next report and reflections.md rather than glossed over. Given the already-confirmed span-level result (gated spans regress far more than the 0.377 aggregate alone suggested, nearly to baseline_replay's level), prediction (2) is plausible enough to take seriously, not dismiss in favor of (1) by default.
hypotheses.required_changes: New retroactive analysis script src/real_time_translation/experiments/soft_anchor_gate_erasure_decomposition.py, zero new API calls: (1) load experiments/20260922_h_soft_anchor_gate_min3_replay.json, restrict to the guest-talk source's spans with non-empty gated_batch_indices (42 spans); (2) for each such span, each repeat (0 and 1), and both the gated_soft_anchor and soft_anchor_replay conditions, take condition_repeats[cond][repeat] (the per-batch cumulative Japanese text list) and compute the per-transition erasure list by reusing flicker_metrics._longest_common_prefix_len directly (do not reimplement LCP) -- erasure_t = len(outs[t]) - lcp(outs[t], outs[t+1]) for t=0..len(outs)-2; (3) label transition t as 'gated_transition' if (t+1) is in that span's gated_batch_indices, else 'nongated_transition_in_gated_span'; (4) for each label, compare gated_soft_anchor's mean erasure_t against soft_anchor_replay's mean erasure_t (report both raw character counts and each transition's erasure_t normalized by that span's own final-text length, consistent with how normalized_erasure() defines the per-span ratio); (5) report the two group comparisons side by side plus per-span detail for the largest few outlier spans (by excess erasure) so a human/future session can spot-check specific examples, not just aggregate numbers. Write output to experiments/soft_anchor_gate_erasure_decomposition.json + a results.csv row per PLAYBOOK.md/CLAUDE.md logging convention, noting explicitly that no new Deepgram/LLM spend occurred (pure retroactive analysis over already-recorded condition_repeats text).
hypotheses.result_summary: Decomposed the 42 guest-talk gated spans into per-transition erasure, labeling each transition gated_transition ((t+1) in gated_batch_indices) vs nongated_transition_in_gated_span, reusing flicker_metrics._longest_common_prefix_len directly. Result: gated_soft_anchor excess normalized erasure over soft_anchor_replay is 0.549 on gated transitions themselves (n=84, mean 0.615 vs 0.067) but only 0.040 on non-gated transitions within the SAME gated spans (n=50, mean 0.077 vs 0.036) -- about 13.6x smaller. This confirms prediction (1) contained re-reveal, not (2) destabilization: the gate's cost is mostly local to the transition it directly holds back, and does not meaningfully propagate into later translation within the same span. One outlier (span 34, 4 nongated transitions, excess 0.358) is well above the rest of the distribution and worth a closer look in a future cycle, but does not change the aggregate conclusion. This resolves the open question h-soft-anchor-gate-min-words-3's result_summary left unanswered: the aggregate guest-talk NE regression (0.377 vs 0.089) is explained by a small number of expensive gated transitions, not a broad quality problem with the gating approach.

hypotheses.title: Does translation_fidelity_judge.judge()'s single holistic 0-100 score hide rubric collapse? Replay a sample of already-judged spans with a new decomposed-rubric prompt (named sub-criteria scores + overall score in the same call) and measure factor correlation / schematic adherence per arxiv2509-20293's method.
hypotheses.description: This cycle's READ_PAPERS cross-reference (see papers.json _read_cross_reference_note_cycle53) revisited two candidate directions cycle 22 flagged from arxiv2509-20293 ('When Judgment Becomes Noise'), arxiv2606-19544 ('Reliability without Validity'), and arxiv2607-02235 (LLM-judge in multilingual/low-resource settings) but never wrote up: (1) applying arxiv2509-20293's 'schematic adherence'/factor-collapse diagnostic to translation_fidelity_judge.judge(), and (2) a human-vs-judge spot-check. Direction (1) as originally framed ('apply retroactively to already-stored outputs') does not work: verified directly against src/real_time_translation/experiments/translation_fidelity_judge.py before finalizing this hypothesis (per PLAYBOOK.md's field-verification rule) that judge() returns a SINGLE holistic 'score' field (one rubric criterion -- information retention), not the multiple named sub-criteria the paper's diagnostic needs to decompose. There is nothing to decompose in data already collected. Reformulated here as a new, small, cheap replay: ask a NEW prompt for 4 named sub-criteria scores (numbers_and_statistics, named_entities_and_technical_terms, causal_logical_relationships, overall_completeness, each 0-100) PLUS the existing holistic 'score' field, all in ONE Gemini call per sampled point (same call-count cost as a plain re-judge, not 4x). Schematic adherence is then computed within that SAME call's own output (R^2 of 'score' regressed on the 4 sub-criteria from the same response), which isolates whether this repo's own rubric is self-coherent without conflating it with cross-call judge noise (cycle 19-21's already-established confound). Also reports pairwise Pearson correlation between the 4 sub-criteria themselves -- per arxiv2509-20293's finding on Arena-Hard Auto, correlations >0.9 across nominally-distinct criteria would mean the new rubric is itself collapsed/not discriminating, a negative but still useful result (would mean decomposing the rubric doesn't buy anything and the existing single-score design is not meaningfully worse).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Two falsifiable outcomes, reported honestly regardless of which the data supports: (A) 'rubric is fine' -- sub-criteria show low-to-moderate pairwise correlation (not all >0.9) AND schematic adherence R^2 is high (the holistic score is well-explained by genuinely distinct sub-criteria), meaning the existing single-score judge is a reasonable summary and decomposing it is not worth the extra complexity going forward. (B) 'rubric collapse' -- sub-criteria are highly inter-correlated (>0.9, mirroring arxiv2509-20293's Arena-Hard Auto finding) and/or schematic adherence R^2 is low, meaning the holistic score is not well-explained by the stated criteria even in its own self-report -- in that case, flag in the next report that past aggregate judge-score comparisons in this backlog (h-masking-holdback, h-soft-anchor-* line, etc.) should be read with the same caution already applied to judge noise (cycle 19-21), now for a validity reason rather than a pure-noise reason, and propose to the human whether the production rubric itself should change.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/judge_schematic_adherence_replay.py. Add a judge_decomposed(source, translation) function (new prompt, same Gemini client/model pattern as translation_fidelity_judge.judge(), model=gemini-3.1-flash-lite) returning {numbers_and_statistics, named_entities_and_technical_terms, causal_logical_relationships, overall_completeness, score} each 0-100 in one JSON response -- do not reuse judge()'s prompt string, write a new one that asks for all 5 fields explicitly. Sample deterministically (not random, for reproducibility) from experiments/20260921_h_soft_anchor_gate_recalibrated_noisefloor_replay.json's by_source spans: for each of the 2 source files, take spans where span_index % 5 == 0 (~20 spans/source, ~60 span-condition points total across baseline_replay/soft_anchor_replay/gated_soft_anchor), repeats[0] only (consistent with judge_verbosity_bias_check.py's convention for the same reason -- avoid conflating repeat noise with this check). For each sampled point, call judge_decomposed(span['source_full'], last cumulative text of condition_repeats[cond][0]). Compute: (1) pairwise Pearson r between the 4 named sub-criteria across all sampled points; (2) within each point's own response, R^2 of 'score' regressed (simple OLS, no external library needed, same style as judge_verbosity_bias_check.py's hand-rolled _pearson_r) on the 4 sub-criteria, reported as a distribution (mean/median R^2 across points is NOT meaningful per-point since 1 observation can't support its own regression -- instead fit ONE pooled OLS of score ~ 4 sub-criteria across all ~60 points and report that single R^2, this is schematic adherence at the rubric level, not per-point). Write experiments/judge_schematic_adherence_replay.json + a results.csv row per CLAUDE.md/PLAYBOOK.md logging convention. Run `uv run ruff check .` on the new file before committing.
hypotheses.result_summary: Ran successfully (60/60 new gemini-3.1-flash-lite decomposed-judge calls, no parse failures, $0.02 logged) but INCONCLUSIVE for the intended schematic-adherence/factor-collapse question, due to a severe ceiling effect in the sampled data, not a flaw in the method itself. Scores: causal_logical_relationships=100 for all 60/60 points (zero variance); numbers_and_statistics and named_entities_and_technical_terms >=80 for 59/60 points each; overall_completeness >=80 for all 60; holistic 'score' >=85 for all 60 (47/60 exactly 100). schematic_adherence_r_squared came back null because the pooled OLS design matrix was singular (the zero-variance causal_logical_relationships column cannot be fit against); 3 of 6 pairwise sub-criteria correlations are also null for the same reason, and the 3 non-null ones (numbers_and_statistics vs overall_completeness, named_entities vs overall_completeness, both r=0.230) are computed from effectively ~10-13 non-ceiling points, too few to trust. Root cause, verified against the actual sampled text (not just reasoned about in the abstract, per PLAYBOOK.md's verification rule): this replay judges the FINAL cumulative per-condition translation text (last entry of condition_repeats[cond][0], same convention judge_verbosity_bias_check.py uses), and by the end of a span, baseline_replay/soft_anchor_replay/gated_soft_anchor have almost always converged to near-complete content regardless of whether gating fired mid-span -- gating in this backlog changes WHEN content is displayed (flicker/erasure/latency), not whether it eventually survives to the final text. That is actually a consistent, reassuring cross-check of this whole soft-anchor/gating line's own framing (h-soft-anchor-*, h-soft-anchor-gate-erasure-decomposition, etc. have always measured flicker/NE, never claimed an information-retention cost) -- it is just the wrong sample for testing THIS particular diagnostic. Does not resolve whether translation_fidelity_judge.judge()'s rubric is schematically coherent; that question remains open. A future replay should sample from spans/sources with documented fidelity cost/variation instead (e.g. h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction's or h-semantic-completeness-gating's experiment JSONs, which have recorded actual dropped-content cases) or judge partial/early-batch text rather than final cumulative text, so the sample actually spans the 0-100 range this diagnostic needs.

hypotheses.title: Retry the schematic-adherence rubric-decomposition check (cycle 53's method) on a sample with a DOCUMENTED, pre-existing fidelity cost, not a ceiling-effect sample
hypotheses.description: Direct follow-up to h-judge-rubric-decomposition-schematic-adherence's cycle-53 result and its own explicit recommendation: that run sampled stride-5 FINAL cumulative text from the soft-anchor-gate corpus and got a degenerate result (causal_logical_relationships=100 for 60/60 points, zero variance; schematic_adherence_r_squared null; OLS design matrix singular) because gating in that backlog only affects WHEN content appears, not whether it survives to the final text -- the wrong sample for a diagnostic that needs real 0-100 spread. This hypothesis reuses the exact same decomposed-rubric method (judge_decomposed()'s prompt, _pairwise_correlations(), _ols_r_squared() from judge_schematic_adherence_replay.py, imported not duplicated) but points it at experiments/20260916_compression_repeated_sampling_segment5.json instead, which already has a DOCUMENTED, measured fidelity cost from a prior cycle, not an assumed one: verified directly against that file before finalizing this hypothesis text (per PLAYBOOK.md's verification rule) -- its 'results' key holds exactly 2 conditions (baseline_replay, compression_actions), each with results[cond]['samples'][i]['translation'] for i in 0..9, all against the SAME fixed source text (input.target_segment_text = \"course. So I think you already know what's\", a repeated-single-segment design, not the by_source/spans/condition_repeats schema the cycle-53 script's _sampled_points() expects -- the new script needs its own, simpler point-extraction function, not a call to the existing one with different arguments). Its own existing metrics already show real, pre-measured variance in exactly the direction needed: truncation_rate_heuristic is 0.0 for baseline_replay vs 0.4 for compression_actions (4/10 repeats dropped a whole clause), and its own small judge spot-check (judge_results, only 3/10 samples per condition in the original run) already scored one compression_actions sample 50 (vs 100 for the rest) for exactly a dropped-clause reason ('course (context is ambiguous)', \"you already know what's\" flagged as dropped_or_distorted) -- i.e. this sample is known, from data already on disk, to span a real score range before any new call is made, the explicit variance pre-check cycle 53's reflections.md entry asked for.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: With a known ~40% severe-truncation subset in compression_actions and a clean, non-truncated baseline_replay, expect overall_completeness and causal_logical_relationships (the two sub-criteria most directly affected by a dropped clause) to show real sub-ceiling variance this time, and expect the pooled OLS (score ~ 4 sub-criteria) to be solvable (non-singular) with a non-null R^2, unlike cycle 53's degenerate result. Two falsifiable outcomes as before: (A) moderate pairwise sub-criteria correlation + high schematic-adherence R^2 -> the rubric is self-coherent even with genuine fidelity variance present, a cleaner positive result than cycle 53 could produce either way; (B) pairwise correlations still collapse to >0.9 despite real variance in the underlying translations -> a STRONGER case for rubric collapse than cycle 53's inconclusive run, since it can no longer be explained away by 'nothing varied in the sample in the first place'.
hypotheses.required_changes: New small script src/real_time_translation/experiments/judge_schematic_adherence_replay_knowncost.py that imports judge_decomposed, _pairwise_correlations, _ols_r_squared, SUB_CRITERIA from judge_schematic_adherence_replay.py (do not duplicate the prompt or stats code) and adds its own point-extraction function reading experiments/20260916_compression_repeated_sampling_segment5.json's input.target_segment_text as the fixed source and results[cond]['samples'][i]['translation'] (both conditions, all 10 repeats each = 20 points total, not just the original run's 3-sample spot-check) as the translation for each point. Call judge_decomposed(source, translation) for all 20 points (20 new gemini-3.1-flash-lite calls, same per-call cost as cycle 53's run), write experiments/judge_schematic_adherence_replay_knowncost.json + a results.csv row per CLAUDE.md/PLAYBOOK.md logging convention, and run `uv run ruff check .` on the new file before committing. Log actual cost via `orchestrator.py log-cost` immediately after the run.
hypotheses.result_summary: Ran successfully (20/20 new gemini-3.1-flash-lite decomposed-judge calls, no parse failures, $0.01 logged), but STILL INCONCLUSIVE for the schematic-adherence/factor-collapse question -- for a different reason than cycle 53. No config drift risk to check here (pure re-judge of already-recorded translation text, no live pipeline/ASR config involved). All 20 sampled points (10 baseline_replay + 10 compression_actions repeats of the single fixed source segment) scored numbers_and_statistics=named_entities_and_technical_terms=causal_logical_relationships=100 and overall_completeness/score=100 for 19/20 (one 90) -- zero sub-ceiling spread again, so pairwise_subcriteria_correlations and schematic_adherence_r_squared are null/singular, same degenerate shape as cycle 53. Verified directly against the source file (not assumed): 3 of the 10 compression_actions repeats (indices 0, 1, 5; output_chars=12, covers_both_clauses_heuristic=False) DO drop the 'course' clause per the source JSON's own truncation_rate_heuristic=0.4, so the predicted variance-bearing cases were genuinely included in this replay's sample -- but this decomposed-rubric judge call scored all three 100 anyway. Root cause (verified against input.target_segment_text and context_lines in the source JSON, not reasoned about abstractly): target_segment_text is an isolated, out-of-context ASR fragment ("course. So I think you already know what's"), and this replay -- like the original replay script it is modeled on -- passes only that fragment as judge_decomposed()'s source, with no context_lines. The judge treats a dropped clause in an already-ambiguous fragment as unrecoverable/unscoreable context rather than a real omission. Notably, this source file's OWN prior 3-sample judge() spot-check (judge_results in the JSON) scored one of these exact same truncated translations 50/100 for dropped content under the SAME context-free framing -- a genuine single-call-vs-decomposed-call judge disagreement on identical inputs, which reads as an instance of the already-established judge-resampling noise (cycle 19-21), not a new flaw in this method. Does not resolve the schematic-adherence question either way; a future attempt should sample multi-segment spans with context_lines included in the judge prompt, so a dropped clause remains scoreable rather than being absorbed into fragment ambiguity.

hypotheses.title: Third attempt at the schematic-adherence/factor-collapse diagnostic, this time on multi-segment sliding-window spans with real context on BOTH sides, sampled from an experiment with an already-documented non-ceiling fidelity difference
hypotheses.description: Direct follow-up to h-judge-rubric-decomposition-schematic-adherence (cycle 53) and h-judge-schematic-adherence-knowncost-resample (cycle 54), both of which got a degenerate zero-variance result (all/nearly-all sub-criteria scores pegged at 100) for two DIFFERENT root causes: cycle 53 sampled FINAL cumulative multi-batch text where conditions had already converged by the end; cycle 54 fixed that by sampling a condition with a real, pre-documented fidelity gap (truncation_rate_heuristic 0.0 vs 0.4), but that sample's source was a single isolated out-of-context ASR fragment ('course. So I think you already know what's'), which the judge treated as unrecoverable fragment ambiguity rather than a scoreable omission -- same degenerate shape, new cause. Cycle 54's own report and reflections.md explicitly recommend the fix: sample multi-segment spans with real surrounding context on both the source and translation side, drawn from an experiment with an already-documented NON-ceiling fidelity difference, not an isolated fragment. experiments/20260916_compression_actions_prompt.json (h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction) fits this precisely: verified directly against the file before finalizing this hypothesis (per PLAYBOOK.md's field-verification rule) that it holds 23 sequential, ordered segments per condition (baseline_replay vs compression_actions) over the SAME 120s clip, each segment carrying its own source_text and translation, and that this experiment's own prior holistic judge() call already scored the two conditions differently on real, named, non-ceiling grounds (retention_score 75 vs 85, with distinct dropped_or_distorted lists per condition -- e.g. baseline_replay misses 'token errors' and 'three based on the', compression_actions introduces a new 'small three' ambiguity but recovers 'token errors'). This is a genuine, already-measured, non-ceiling fidelity difference with full surrounding context available, unlike both prior attempts.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Using a 4-segment sliding window (source_text and translation of segments [i, i+3] concatenated with spaces, for i = 0..19, giving 20 overlapping context-bearing spans per condition, 40 points total -- window size chosen so every window spans multiple clauses/sentences, giving the judge real surrounding context, while still keeping windows containing segment index 5 (the documented dropped/distorted region) distinct from mostly-clean windows elsewhere in the clip), expect REAL variance in sub-criteria scores this time, concentrated in named_entities_and_technical_terms and overall_completeness for windows overlapping segment 5, not pegged at 100 everywhere. Two falsifiable outcomes either way: (A) if windows show real score spread and pairwise sub-criteria correlations are not all >0.9 AND schematic_adherence_r_squared is a real, non-null number -- the rubric-decomposition diagnostic is finally usable on this repo's data, and the R^2/correlation values themselves become the actual finding (first real answer to the question this hypothesis line has asked for 2 cycles). (B) if scores are STILL pegged at 100 even for windows overlapping the documented drops, that would be a stronger finding than either prior cycle's -- it would mean gemini-3.1-flash-lite's decomposed-judge call specifically (not just context-starved samples) under-penalizes the kinds of drops this repo's experiments actually produce, worth flagging plainly to the human rather than attempting a 4th resample.
hypotheses.required_changes: New small script src/real_time_translation/experiments/judge_schematic_adherence_replay_context_windows.py that imports judge_decomposed, _pairwise_correlations, _ols_r_squared, SUB_CRITERIA from judge_schematic_adherence_replay.py (do not duplicate the prompt or stats code, same reuse pattern as cycle 54's knowncost-resample script) and adds its own point-extraction function reading experiments/20260916_compression_actions_prompt.json's results[cond]['segments'] list (23 segments per condition, ordered by 'index'), building sliding windows of 4 consecutive segments (i=0..19), joining each window's 'source_text' values with a space for source_full and 'translation' values with a space for translation_full, for both conditions (baseline_replay, compression_actions) = 40 points total. Calls judge_decomposed(source_full, translation_full) once per point (40 new Gemini calls, gemini-3.1-flash-lite, zero new Deepgram spend), writes rows + pairwise_subcriteria_correlations + schematic_adherence_r_squared to experiments/judge_schematic_adherence_replay_context_windows.json and a flat CSV, same output shape as judge_schematic_adherence_replay.py. Must log-cost after running (uv run ruff check . before commit).
hypotheses.result_summary: CONCLUSIVE, unlike cycles 53 and 54: sampling 4-segment sliding windows (joining source_text/translation across the window, 20 windows per condition = 40 points) from experiments/20260916_compression_actions_prompt.json finally produced real, non-degenerate variance. Per-window scores range the full 0-100 scale in named_entities_and_technical_terms, causal_logical_relationships and overall_completeness (numbers_and_statistics stays near-100 throughout -- this source clip simply has almost no numeric content to drop). Low-scoring windows (window_start 7-10 and 17-19 in both conditions) are not judge noise: verified directly against the source JSON's segments that these windows cover genuinely disfluent/garbled ASR source text ('we just have a small three', 'token errors', 'FFN layer. Normally, FFN layer' repeated twice in a row at segments 21/22), matching the same spans this experiment's own prior holistic judge() call already flagged via dropped_or_distorted ('token errors', 'small three', 'three based on the'). Diagnostics: (1) pairwise sub-criteria correlations are NOT all >0.9 -- numbers_and_statistics vs the other 3 criteria is near-zero or slightly negative (-0.09 to 0.07, it has almost no variance to correlate with), named_entities vs causal_logical/overall_completeness is moderate (0.51/0.62), and only causal_logical_relationships vs overall_completeness is high (0.95) -- plausible, since a dropped causal link usually also reduces overall completeness in the same window. (2) schematic_adherence_r_squared=0.996, a real, non-null, very high value: the holistic 'score' field is almost entirely explained by the 4 named sub-criteria within the same call, i.e. this repo's rubric is schematically coherent on this sample, not collapsed. Net finding: the decomposed-rubric diagnostic from arxiv2509-20293 is usable on this repo's judge, but only when given (a) multi-clause real context on both source and translation sides and (b) a sample that actually contains quality-varying content (disfluent/garbled source regions, not a clip that is uniformly easy or uniformly hard) -- confirms the two root causes diagnosed in cycles 53 and 54 respectively were both real and are now both avoided. This result is specific to this one clip's disfluency pattern; it does not establish whether holistic score vs sub-criteria correlation structure generalizes to other clips/domains.

hypotheses.title: Human review 'duplicate captions': drop already-emitted words by a persistent audio-time watermark on Deepgram word timings
hypotheses.description: Human review of the full LLM2024_8_part1 captions (experiments/20260924_llm2024_8_part1_human_review.md) reported frequent duplicate captions. In 20260918_llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict.json 177/1209 (14.6%) final segments start before the end of an already-emitted segment (e.g. seg 59/60 'Gemma 3D, Gemma four stuffs. Okay.' then 'Gemma 3D, Gemma four stuffs.'). Root cause: deepgram_client.py dedups only by per-utterance word COUNT, reset on UtteranceEnd/is_final; an UtteranceEnd flush of the pending interim followed by Deepgram's late is_final for the same audio (or re-segmentation of a trailing word) re-emits the words as a new utterance.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: overlap_duplicate_rate (caption_issue_metrics.py) drops from ~0.14 to <0.03 on the same window, with no increase in empty/missing speech.
hypotheses.required_changes: deepgram_client.py: TranscriptionResult.words (per-word timings), _take_unemitted() trimming leading words whose end <= _emitted_until (never reset per utterance, reset on connect). Falls back to count-only when word list and transcript don't align 1:1. Unit tests in tests/test_caption_review_fixes.py.
hypotheses.result_summary: PARTIALLY CONFIRMED. Same window (450-1310s) live rerun v2: overlap_duplicate_rate 13.6% -> 3.8% (33/243 -> 9/234), no empty translations. Raw Deepgram message debug on the 07:30 audio then showed the residual cause: Deepgram sends UtteranceEnd BEFORE the is_final of the same segment, and the final's word timings are wider than the interim's (everyone. 8.25-8.57 -> 8.41-8.97), so neither end-time nor midpoint watermark catches it. v3 fix (restore consumed word count when the flushed segment start reappears) verified on that 20s of live audio + unit test, but the full-window v3 run was blocked twice by local network loss (DNS failure / Deepgram WS close) -- not yet measured. See experiments/20260924_llm2024_8_part1_human_review.md section 4.2.

hypotheses.title: Human review 'JoshAnguo / Muscle Lab / Suspension-Agent': ASR-alias dictionary column + fuzzy retrieval + prompt rule-4 ASR-error exception
hypotheses.description: Human review (experiments/20260924_llm2024_8_part1_human_review.md) reported misheard names left uncorrected. hypotheses.title: Are the human-perceived 'translation skips / dropped clauses' sub-second cards and low-confidence ASR spans rather than API limits?
hypotheses.description: Human review (experiments/20260924_llm2024_8_part1_human_review.md) asked whether skips were API limits. Baseline evidence: 0/1209 empty translations, no timeouts recorded, over-compression (<1 JA char per EN word) only 0.5% -- but 25.1% of cards display <1s and the Chinchilla passage (seg 221) had ASR confidence 0.47.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Aligning the reviewer's timestamps of perceived skips with cue durations and ASR confidence explains most of them; the post-fix run has fewer sub-second cards and so fewer perceived skips.
hypotheses.required_changes: Needs the reviewer's timestamps (or a second viewing of the post-fix render) -- $0 analysis over existing JSON otherwise.
experiment_ids: retroactive: src/real_time_translation/experiments/perceived_drop_analysis.py (new module) run over all 96 experiments/*.json with a results.events log -- see experiments/perceived_drop_analysis.csv
hypotheses.result_summary: retroactive_cue_outcome_replay (no reviewer timestamps were available beyond the human review note's few named examples, so the analysis uses low ASR confidence (<0.6) as the review's own proxy for a 'felt like a drop' spot, per review item E, plus a new, independently-derived signal: whether a segment's final translation ever became ITS OWN visible on-screen cue at all, replaying render_honest_captions.build_cues's exact cut logic keyed per segment). RESULT: the hypothesis's PREDICTED mechanism (sub-second cards + low ASR confidence) is NOT the dominant explanation -- shown_but_under_1s was 0 in every one of the 96 experiments checked (this repo's cue hold-time minimum, 0.6s plus a further +1.2s for most segments since nearly all of them end an utterance in this fragmented-ASR corpus, floors every SHOWN cue's duration at 1.8s+ in practice, so 'shown but briefly' essentially never happens) and low confidence is rare (101/8343 = 1.2% pooled) with little overlap with any display issue (only 19/101 = 18.8% also invisible-or-short). Instead, a third, much larger, PREVIOUSLY UNDOCUMENTED mechanism dominates: a segment's final translation can be fully correct and never shown on screen at all, because a closely-following segment's text overwrites the pending cue before this segment's own minimum hold time elapses -- found in 2488/8343 = 29.8% of segments pooled across all 96 experiments (21.75% on the human-reviewed full lecture itself, experiments/20260918_llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict.json, 262 of the 263 affected segments there are themselves utterance-final, not mid-sentence growth being superseded by its own later text). This content is NOT actually dropped from the system (it is present in full_translation and in results.segments) -- it is a RENDERING-level loss, invisible to the viewer, which plausibly reads exactly like '翻訳飛ばし' (skipped translation) despite 0/1209 empty translations and no API timeouts, confirming review item E's 'not API limit' conclusion via a completely independent mechanism. The rate tracks utterance-fragmentation volume directly: runs with many short, closely-spaced utterances (asr_keyterms_off 70%, llm2024_8_part1_full 36.5%) swallow far more segments than runs with fewer, longer batches (raised-timer/semantic-gating hypothesis test runs, ~5%), i.e. it is a direct consequence of the same over-fragmentation already root-caused by review items A/F and partly mitigated by h-review-asr-reemission-watermark/h-review-dangling-connective-carry's fixes -- the review_fixes_v2 run (same fix set, different clip region, NOT a strictly controlled before/after since segment counts and window differ: 234 segments / 860s vs. 1209 segments / full lecture) shows a lower never-shown rate (16.24%) than the original run (21.75%), directionally consistent with but not proof of the fixes helping this specific metric. CONCLUSION: the hypothesis's top-level claim (perceived drops are not API limits) is CONFIRMED, but its proposed MECHANISM is subordinate -- the dominant cause is this cue-overwrite/never-shown effect, not short display duration or low confidence, which should be the next hypothesis's target (e.g. a floor on how often the pending cue is allowed to be silently replaced before being shown at all, independent of its own min-hold timer).

hypotheses.title: Compute IWSLT-comparable, character-level, computation-aware LAAL/StreamLAAL for existing runs, and place this cascade next to SimulSeamless's En->Ja operating point
hypotheses.description: quality_latency_joint.py deliberately skipped AL/LAAL/YAAL because 'token-level source-consumption formulas need per-token source-alignment data this pipeline's event log does not carry'. For SPEECH input, though, SimulEval's AL/LAAL (and StreamLAAL/LongYAAL) define each target unit's delay as the elapsed source-audio time when it was emitted. No token alignment is needed, only an emission timestamp on the source-audio clock. Verified 2026-09-24: all 94 experiment JSONs that carry results.events have a playback_offset field on their events, including translation_partial/translation_complete. So each emitted Japanese character has a computation-aware delay (it includes Deepgram, queueing and LLM wall time). Compute character-level LAAL/StreamLAAL per experiment: re-segment the emitted JA stream against reference segments, using experiments/refs/wjZofJX0v4M.ja.vtt (it has timings) for the wjZofJX0v4M clips, or per ASR utterance as a fallback. Add the columns to the joint table. The point is an external yardstick: IWSLT 2024 En->Ja SimulSeamless reports BLEU 22.19 @ AL 1.997s with computation-aware AL 4.018s. This repo's only latency numbers today are its own avg_end_to_end_latency, CLA and MT decomposition, none of which is comparable to the literature. Per PLAYBOOK, check before implementing whether a partial event's playback_offset is the time the batch was received or the time of the first token.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: No system change (measurement only). Expect computation-aware char-level LAAL of roughly 5-7s on the lecture runs (translation_complete wall_clock_lag median 6.17s on 20260918_llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict), i.e. ~1.5x SimulSeamless's 4.0s ca-AL. That would place the gap in commit/queue policy rather than ASR, consistent with h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition. Caveat: MuST-C is pre-segmented TED and IWSLT uses BLEU, so this is a positioning number, not a head-to-head comparison.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/simul_latency_metrics.py (console script), plus an extra join in quality_latency_joint.py. No pipeline changes. Follow ufal/asr_latency or SimulEval's LAAL definition exactly, and unit-test it against a hand-computed toy example.
hypotheses.result_summary: Implemented src/real_time_translation/experiments/simul_latency_metrics.py: character-level, computation-aware Average Lagging (AL), adapted for speech source (no token-alignment needed, confirmed before implementing per PLAYBOOK's standing instruction). Validated against 5 hand-computed toy unit tests (constant-offset and zero-lag cases both land exactly on the expected analytic value). Ran over all 102 experiment JSONs that carry results.events; joined ca_al_char_s / ca_al_vtt_refrate_char_s into quality_latency_joint.py. RESULT: prediction partially confirmed, with an important caveat found during implementation. Raw corpus-wide mean ca_al_char_s=3.98s (n=102) lands close to SimulSeamless's cited computation-aware AL of 4.018s, but this is misleading on inspection: anchoring the ideal-rate line at the clip's t=0 (not speech start) made every number wildly wrong (mean was -6.0s, range -271..+237s) because of ~75s of lead-in dead air before the first utterance in several runs -- fixed by anchoring to [first_asr_start_time, last_asr_end_time] instead (documented in the module). After that fix, the two nominally-identical 'full lecture' runs diverge sharply: llm2024_8_part1_full/_baseline_no_dict give -0.41s/15.06s (in literature range) while llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture(_v2_dict) give 179-199s -- traced to that specific recording's own internal pause structure (top gaps 104s/90s/55s vs the other lecture's max 8.2s gap; 16% vs 9.4% of total runtime is silence), not a code bug: this is exactly the segmentation/pause-sensitivity polak2026-meta-evaluation-latency-metrics (SOFTSEGMENTER) argues naive AL has for long-form audio, now confirmed empirically on this repo's own data, not just read from a paper. Excluding the two multi-hour runs and tiny-output edge cases (n=93, 90-860s clips, >=200 output chars): mean=0.58s, median=0.68s, stdev=10.2s -- still far too noisy per-experiment to support precise head-to-head numbers, but moderate-length runs with substantial output (asr_keyterms_on 39.9s/1114 chars, llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min 33.0s/2783 chars) sit roughly 10-40s, an order of magnitude above SimulSeamless's 4.018s dedicated end-to-end model -- plausible given this is an API cascade with batched LLM calls and a commit-policy queue, consistent with h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition's own queue-wait findings. The separate VTT-reference-rate column (ca_al_vtt_refrate_char_s, deliberately NOT named LAAL) came out counter-intuitively MORE negative than the self-rate AL given this pipeline's JA output is longer than the reference caption -- the opposite of what Papi et al.'s actual over-generation correction should do -- flagged in the module docstring as unverified against the primary source, not to be trusted yet.

hypotheses.title: Small human Continuous Rating session: does the Netflix 4-CPS (kanji x2) reading-time target actually match what a live viewer wants, vs a Subtitler-style 6-8 CPS?
hypotheses.description: Two gaps meet here. (1) No human Continuous Rating (Machacek & Bojar 2020) has ever been collected. Machacek et al. 2023 show offline metrics correlate with it, but this repo's chrF/xCOMET/LLM-judge scores have never been checked against a human on Japanese output; arxiv2607-02235 flags exactly this human-validation gap. (2) The caption scheduler targets Netflix's offline-subtitling norm of 4 CPS with kanji weighted 2x. The median cps_violation_rate across caption_readability_from_experiment.csv is 1.0, and the 2026-09-15 sweep concluded that no setting gets both low lag and Netflix-grade CPS. Subtitler uses an adaptive 10-25 CPS, and Sasaki 2017 questions the 4-CPS norm, so the target may simply be wrong for live lecture captions. Protocol: re-render the SAME experiment JSON (20260918_llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict, a 5-10 min excerpt) at reading_units_per_sec=4 vs 8 (catchup_window unchanged), with no new API calls. rm-2278 watches both in randomized order and gives a 1-4 rating every ~5s (a simple keypress logger). Then correlate the per-window ratings with the per-window caption lag, CPS, and judge()/chrF over the same windows.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: reading_units_per_sec=8 is rated equal or better than 4, because lower queueing lag outweighs slightly faster text. Per-window rating correlates more with lag than with CPS. Judge/chrF correlate positively but weakly (n is small, one rater). Also gives the first human anchor for the LLM judge's Japanese scoring.
hypotheses.required_changes: A tiny keypress-logging rating tool (a script, or a page that plays the mp4 and records timestamped 1-4 keys) plus re-render via caption_video_demo with reading_units_per_sec overridden. No pipeline or API changes. Needs roughly 20-30 min of human viewing time.

hypotheses.title: Show a faded provisional line (English interim ASR) while the Japanese translation is pending, to cut time-to-first-visible-text from ~6s to ~1s
hypotheses.description: On 20260918_llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict (measured 2026-09-24), the first asr_interim event for an ASR start time arrives a median 1.17s (p90 2.11s) after that start time. The first translation text arrives a median 6.01s (p90 6.40s) after it. The two were computed separately, not as a joined per-utterance pair. So viewers see nothing new for ~5s while the speaker is already talking. MeetDot fades unstable text instead of hiding it, Subtitler shows unstable tails, and Machacek 2023 finds viewers who know the source language prefer lower latency over fewer revisions. Proposal: the overlay shows the in-progress English interim in a small, dimmed line below the committed Japanese card, replaced when that utterance's translation lands. This costs $0 in LLM calls (no provisional translation) and does not touch the Japanese caption's stability (translation NE unchanged). A provisional Japanese translation of the interim is a costlier follow-up, not part of this hypothesis. Step 1 ($0, retroactive): per utterance, compute the time-to-first-visible-text distribution with and without the preview, plus English-line flicker (word-level NE of asr_interim, already ~0.20 per flicker_metrics). Step 2: overlay.html change behind a flag, then a viewing check (can piggyback on h-continuous-rating-cps-calibration).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Time-to-first-visible-text drops by ~4-5s median. The dimmed English line has asr NE ~0.2 (it visibly rewrites), which is acceptable only if it is visually secondary. Expect a net positive for English-literate viewers and neutral or slightly negative for others, which is why it sits behind a flag.
hypotheses.required_changes: Retroactive analysis script ($0). Later, web/overlay.html and live_presenter.py: pass asr_interim text through as a separate 'preview' channel behind a config flag. Note overlay.html currently has uncommitted human edits, so coordinate before touching it.
experiment_ids: retroactive: all experiments/*.json with a results.events list (97 files)
hypotheses.result_summary: Step 1 implemented: src/real_time_translation/experiments/interim_preview_timing.py (console script not registered in pyproject.toml, run via python3 -m, same precedent as soft_anchor_*/judge_* scripts), joining per-utterance (grouped by asr_start_time, same key as flicker_metrics.group_asr_interim/group_translation_by_utterance) the first asr_interim event wall_clock_lag against the first translation_partial/translation_complete event wall_clock_lag for the SAME utterance, reusing TimedEvent's own wall_clock_lag field (playback_offset - asr_start_time) directly rather than recomputing it. /bin/bash spent, no new Deepgram/LLM calls -- pure retroactive analysis over all 97 experiments/*.json with event logs, written to experiments/interim_preview_timing.csv. CONFIRMED on the specific experiment the hypothesis cited (20260918_llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict): time_to_first_interim median=1.166s p90=2.105s; time_to_first_translation median=6.035s p90=6.396s -- both essentially identical to the hypothesis's own informal estimates (1.17s/2.11s and 6.01s/6.40s), validating that those earlier numbers were not a fluke of ad-hoc computation. Properly JOINED per-utterance preview_gain_s (translation_lag - interim_lag) on that same experiment has median=4.321s, mean=3.822s -- close to but not identical to the naive separately-computed-medians subtraction (6.035-1.166=4.869s) the hypothesis implicitly assumed, because the two underlying distributions are not independent per utterance (short/fast utterances skew both lags together). Across the FULL corpus (97 experiments, 6638 utterances with both sides present, not just the one cited clip), the effect generalizes: pooled-across-utterances preview_gain_s median=3.662s mean=5.024s (mean of per-experiment medians=6.651s, i.e. individual experiments vary a lot but the gain is positive and multi-second in essentially every one). English-line flicker (word-level NE of the would-be preview line, reusing flicker_metrics.group_asr_interim directly): corpus mean=0.189, matching the hypothesis's cited 'already ~0.20 per flicker_metrics' figure closely. CONCLUSION: the hypothesis's core premise -- that an English interim preview would let viewers see something several seconds earlier than the Japanese translation, at the cost of a visibly-revising (NE~0.19) line -- is confirmed with a proper, reproducible, corpus-wide joined measurement, not just the single informally-eyeballed experiment. Step 2 (the actual overlay.html change behind a flag, and the human viewing check) is NOT done in this cycle -- out of scope for this bounded unit of work, and overlay.html has pre-existing uncommitted-elsewhere human edits per the hypothesis's own note, so it should be coordinated with rm-2278 before touching it.

hypotheses.title: Guarantee every finalized segment at least one visible frame in build_cues's cut logic, without just converting the invisibility problem into a milder flicker problem
hypotheses.description: h-review-perceived-drops-short-cards (cycle 57) found that render_honest_captions.build_cues silently discards a pending cue's text with ZERO screen time whenever a closely-following segment's text arrives before the pending cue's own min-hold timer (_hold_for: 0.6s floor, +1.2s more if utterance-end) elapses -- the code just overwrites cue_text/cue_is_end and `continue`s, with no Cue ever appended for the superseded text. Measured: 2488/8343 = 29.8% of segments pooled across all 96 experiments/*.json, 263/1209 = 21.75% on the human-reviewed full lecture itself, 262 of those 263 themselves utterance-final (not mid-sentence growth being superseded by its own later revision). The content is not lost from the system (full_translation/results.segments still have it) -- it is a pure rendering-level loss, and plausibly what the human reviewer perceived as skipped translations. This hypothesis asks the obvious follow-up question raised in cycle 57's reflections.md and NOT yet answered: can build_cues guarantee at least one visible cue per finalized segment, and if so, what does that cost? Specifically, does forcing a short cue for the superseded text (at the min_display_seconds=0.6s floor only, deliberately WITHOUT the +1.2s utterance-end extension, since re-applying full hold time to every forced interstitial cue would just push the overwrite problem one segment further down the queue instead of fixing it) just convert a 'never shown' segment into a 'shown but under SHORT_CUE_SECONDS=1.0s' segment -- the exact flicker-adjacent failure mode that h-review-perceived-drops-short-cards found was 0/8343 (0%) under the CURRENT algorithm specifically because nothing short-lived is ever produced today (things are either fully held for 1.8s+ or not shown at all, with no middle case). If so, this is not a clean win -- it trades an invisible-content problem for a different, milder but real flicker problem, and that tradeoff (plus the cumulative display-timeline lag the forced cues add) is what needs to be measured and reported honestly, per persistent-delivery2026-revision-optimization's broader point that crediting 'currently visible' text is not the same as crediting content a viewer actually perceives well.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Forcing a 0.6s-floor-only cue for every segment that would otherwise be silently overwritten will drive never_shown_as_own_cue toward 0% but will raise shown_but_under_1s from its current ~0% to a substantial, non-trivial rate (plausibly in the same ballpark as the 29.8%/21.75% it replaces, since most previously-invisible segments are exactly the ones that arrive faster than the 0.6-1.8s hold window). Net honest conclusion is likely 'converts the problem, does not remove it' rather than a clean fix -- report whichever outcome the numbers actually show, including the cumulative added end-of-clip lag from the forced extensions, rather than forcing a positive framing.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/cue_minimum_visibility_replay.py, built the same way perceived_drop_analysis.py was (a near-literal, key-tracking copy of build_cues's cut loop, not a call into build_cues itself, so per-segment outcomes stay attributable): when a pending cue would be overwritten before `_hold_for(cue_text, cue_is_end)` elapses AND the new text differs from the pending text, emit a forced Cue capped at `min_display_seconds` (0.6s, no utterance_end_hold_seconds) for the superseded text before starting the new cue's clock, pushing the following cue's effective start out by that forced duration. Re-run over all 96 experiments/*.json (same corpus perceived_drop_analysis.py used) and report, per experiment and pooled: new never_shown_as_own_cue rate, new shown_but_under_1s rate (the key risk metric above), and total added end-of-clip lag in seconds from the forced extensions. Compare directly against experiments/perceived_drop_analysis.csv's existing numbers for the same files. Purely retroactive replay of already-saved results.events -- no new Deepgram/LLM calls, no code change to the live pipeline or to build_cues itself (this stays a standalone analysis script until/unless the human decides the tradeoff is worth shipping).
experiment_ids: retroactive: src/real_time_translation/experiments/cue_minimum_visibility_replay.py run over all 102 experiments/*.json with a results.events log -- see experiments/cue_minimum_visibility_replay.csv
hypotheses.result_summary: CONFIRMED, but the predicted tradeoff is real and the naive implementation has a second, worse failure mode not anticipated in the prediction. (1) The predicted conversion effect IS what happens: pooled across 102 experiments (8577 segments, up from cycle 57's 96/8343 since more runs landed since), never_shown_as_own_cue drops from 29.8% to 1.49% (128/8577) and on the human-reviewed full lecture itself from 21.75% to 0.99% (12/1209) -- but shown_but_under_1s, which was 0% under the current algorithm, jumps to 42.03% pooled (3605/8577) and 31.84% on the full lecture (385/1209), essentially 1:1 with the forced-cue count. So this does NOT remove the display-loss problem, it converts most of it from 'invisible' to 'visible but flashes by in well under 1s' -- not a clean fix, confirming the hypothesis's own predicted_effect almost exactly. The residual 1.49%/0.99% never-shown (not literally 0%) traces to a small number of short connective-phrase segments (e.g. そして/ですので/はい) whose final segment-level translation text doesn't line up with any single tracked event key -- a known approximation limit shared with h-review-perceived-drops-short-cards's original replay, not a new bug. (2) UNANTICIPATED and more serious: the forced-cue approach pushes the *virtual* display clock forward independently of real event arrival time, and because build_cues's cut decision (and this replay's, by design, to stay faithful to it) operates per EVENT, not per finalized segment, every individual token-level partial-text delta that arrives faster than the hold window also gets force-flashed and also pushes the clock -- not just genuine between-segment overwrites. For experiments/20260806_hardest_5min_gpt54nano.json (a dense token-streaming config, 1806 translation events across only 69 segments, i.e. ~26 partial updates per segment), 100% of its 69 segments ended up forced, and the compounding per-event pushes left the virtual clock 553.1s behind real time by the end of a 294.7s clip -- i.e. the caption track would end up displaying content from a point over twice the clip's own length in the past. Two smaller experiments (20260915_latest_model_gpt54mini.json, 20260915_caption_demo_openai_real.json) show the same pattern at a smaller scale (150-170s drift on ~16-segment clips). The full lecture itself and most other experiments show ~0s end-of-clip drift (the virtual clock gets caught up by ordinary utterance-boundary pauses), so this failure mode is specific to configs/models with dense sub-segment partial-token streaming, not a universal problem -- but it is severe exactly where it occurs. CONCLUSION: guaranteeing visibility by pushing the clock forward, applied at the event level (the natural, minimal-diff way to patch build_cues), is not a safe general fix -- it trades one display-loss mode for a milder one on coarse-batch/sentence-level streams, but can catastrophically desync the caption timeline on fine-grained/token-streaming configs. A viable version would need to force visibility only at genuine finalized-segment boundaries (distinguished from within-segment partial growth, e.g. by only forcing when the overwritten text belongs to a DIFFERENT (asr_start_time, asr_end_time) key, not merely different text under the same key) rather than at every event -- left as a natural next hypothesis rather than implemented now, since this cycle's unit of work is this measurement, not a second implementation attempt. Marked tested, not abandoned: the measurement is sound and conclusive, the naive fix strategy is what's rejected.

hypotheses.title: Exclude large mid-run silence gaps from ca_al_char_s's ideal-rate line (SOFTSEGMENTER-style gap exclusion for long-form audio)
hypotheses.description: h-computation-aware-laal-enja's own result_summary found that simul_latency_metrics.py's lead-in/trail-off fix (anchoring the ideal-rate line to [first_asr_start_time, last_asr_end_time]) leaves MID-run pauses unmodeled, and that this is not a hypothetical concern: the two nominally-identical 'full lecture' runs diverge sharply purely because of internal pause structure -- llm2024_8_part1_full/_baseline_no_dict land in the literature-comparable range (-0.41s/15.06s) while llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture(_v2_dict) come out at 179-199s, traced to that recording's own top gaps of 104s/90s/55s (16% of total runtime silence) vs. the other lecture's max 8.2s gap (9.4% silence). Right now every mid-run silent gap counts fully against both the elapsed-time denominator S and every subsequent settle time d_i, so a long natural pause inflates AL even though no translation work is actually backlogged during it -- exactly the long-form segmentation-sensitivity polak2026-meta-evaluation-latency-metrics (SOFTSEGMENTER) argues naive AL/LAAL-style metrics have, now confirmed empirically on this repo's own data rather than only read from the paper (as the module docstring already notes verbatim). Propose: re-map the ideal-rate line to 'speech-present time' by excluding the portion of any inter-utterance gap beyond a data-derived threshold K from both S and every downstream d_i (i.e. treat an excluded gap as if the ideal-rate clock paused during it, shifting every later checkpoint back by the cumulative excluded duration) -- a simplified, single-system, single-condition approximation of SOFTSEGMENTER's segmentation-robust framing, NOT a reimplementation of that paper's actual (cross-system, reference-aware) algorithm; label it accordingly in the module docstring and CSV column name, same caution this module already applies to ca_al_vtt_refrate_char_s's own disclaimer. Per PLAYBOOK's standing instruction to verify empirical claims against the actual data rather than reasoning abstractly: K must be derived from this corpus's own inter-utterance gap distribution (e.g. the natural-pause range seen across the n=93 well-behaved runs from h-computation-aware-laal-enja's own filtered set, vs. the two outlier lecture gaps of 55-104s), not picked as a round number, and the chosen value plus the percentile/rationale behind it must be written into the module docstring.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Excluding mid-run silence beyond threshold K should pull the two outlier full-lecture runs' ca_al_char_s down from ~179-199s toward something in the -0.41s/15.06s range already seen on the structurally similar other lecture, while leaving the n=93 well-behaved runs' numbers roughly unchanged (their own max gap, 8.2s, is expected to sit below K). Two honest outcomes are possible and should both be reported plainly rather than assuming the favorable one: either (a) the inflation on those two runs turns out to be ~entirely a pause/segmentation artifact, supporting polak2026's general claim, or (b) a genuine residual gap remains even after exclusion, meaning some of the 179-199s reflects a real pipeline effect (e.g. a translation backlog that built up before the pause and did not fully drain) rather than pure measurement artifact -- in which case that residual, not the raw pre-exclusion number, is the more honest figure to carry forward into the Japanese report and quality_latency_joint.py.
hypotheses.required_changes: In-place addition to src/real_time_translation/experiments/simul_latency_metrics.py: a new gap-exclusion remap function (operating on the per-span settle-time timeline before the existing AL computation), a new CSV/report column (name it to make clear it is NOT LAAL/SOFTSEGMENTER proper, e.g. ca_al_char_s_gapexcl), and the empirical threshold derivation plus its rationale written into the module docstring in the same style as the existing 'Leading/trailing silence' note. Join the new column into quality_latency_joint.py alongside the existing ca_al_char_s. Add unit tests for the gap-exclusion remap with hand-computed toy examples, analogous to settle_times()'s own worked examples. Purely retroactive re-analysis of the same 102 existing experiment JSONs -- no new Deepgram/LLM calls, no pipeline code change.
hypotheses.result_summary: PARTIALLY CONFIRMED, with an honest residual the predicted_effect flagged as a possible outcome. Implemented mid-run gap exclusion (10s threshold, empirically derived: every one of the other 100 experiment JSONs has a max inter-utterance gap of <=8.25s, while only the two outlier full-lecture runs have gaps >10s, 7-8 of them each, 12.0-103.76s) in simul_latency_metrics.py, re-ran over all 102 experiment JSONs. RESULT: the two previously-anomalous runs drop substantially -- llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture 179.24s -> 59.70s (8 gaps excluded, 239.17s total excluded), llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict 199.32s -> 73.75s (7 gaps, 251.17s excluded) -- confirming most of the original inflation WAS a pure pause/segmentation artifact, as polak2026-meta-evaluation-latency-metrics predicts for naive AL on long-form audio. However the gap-excluded values (59.70s/73.75s) do NOT come down into the structurally-similar other lecture pair's range (-0.41s/15.06s) -- a large residual (~45-70s beyond that range) remains even after excluding every >10s silence. This is the "genuine residual" branch of the two predicted outcomes, not the "pure artifact" branch: some of this pipeline's own latency on these two runs is real, not measurement noise -- plausibly a translation backlog that does not fully drain across/after a long pause (the MT queue may still be working through pre-gap backlog when speech resumes), which would connect to h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition's own queue-wait findings but was not directly measured here (left for a future hypothesis, not chased in this cycle's unit of work). Verified the fix is precisely targeted: all other 100 runs have num_excluded_gaps=0 and ca_al_char_s_gapexcl byte-identical to ca_al_char_s (checked programmatically, not just spot-checked). Added 4 new unit tests (_excluded_gaps/_gap_exclusion_offset toy cases, an end-to-end hand-computed gap-exclusion case verifying 6.5s -> 1.5s on a synthetic 50s-gap toy, and a no-gap case confirming byte-identical output) alongside the existing 5; all 9 pass, full suite (38 tests) passes, ruff clean. No pipeline code touched, no new Deepgram/LLM calls -- pure retroactive re-analysis, \/bin/bash spend.

hypotheses.title: Measure whether batches immediately after a long mid-run silence gap carry an elevated MT queue-wait (explaining h-ca-al-gap-exclusion-softsegmenter's unresolved AL residual)
hypotheses.description: h-ca-al-gap-exclusion-softsegmenter (cycle 61) found that excluding the two outlier full-lecture runs' long mid-run silence gaps (>10s) from ca_al_char_s's ideal-rate line drops their AL substantially (179.24s->59.70s, 199.32s->73.75s) but leaves a 45-70s residual that does NOT come down into the structurally similar other lecture pair's range (-0.41s/15.06s), and speculated this residual could be 'a translation backlog that does not fully drain across/after a long pause', connectable to h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition's own queue_wait_s metric but not directly measured there. This hypothesis measures that directly and retroactively, no new API calls: for each of the two outlier runs, use simul_latency_metrics._asr_utterance_intervals()/_excluded_gaps() (GAP_EXCLUSION_THRESHOLD_S=10.0) to get the exact gap boundaries (verified cycle 62: 8 gaps/239.17s for llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture, 7 gaps/251.17s for _v2_dict -- the module docstring's prior '6 gaps each' claim was stale and has been corrected in the same commit as this hypothesis), then join against mt_latency_decomposition.batch_latencies()'s per-batch queue_wait_s keyed by the same (asr_start_time, asr_end_time) used throughout this codebase, tagging each batch as 'first batch whose asr_start_time falls within ~1s of a gap's gap_end' (post-gap) vs. everything else (baseline), then compare the two groups' queue_wait_s distributions within each run and against each run's own overall median/mean.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: A quick exploratory check during this GENERATE_HYPOTHESES cycle (not yet a formal experiment run, but run against the real data to verify this hypothesis is worth queuing per PLAYBOOK's standing instruction) already shows a large, consistent effect: across the 11 post-gap batches with a resolvable queue_wait_s (5 of 8 gaps in the first run, 6 of 7 in the second -- the remaining gaps have no batch whose asr_interim content-ready timestamp the lookup can resolve, a known limitation of mt_latency_decomposition._content_ready_lookup() carried over unchanged from h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition, not something this hypothesis's required_changes need to fix to get a usable answer), queue_wait_s is 7.43-8.47s (one outlier at 2.57s, one at 2.80s), versus each run's own overall median of 1.17-1.23s / mean of 1.40-1.50s across ~220 batches -- roughly a 5-7x elevation. Expect the formal run to confirm this pattern holds for all/most resolvable post-gap batches (not just a cherry-picked few) and to quantify how much of the 45-70s AL residual this queueing effect alone can account for (e.g. summing each gap's post-gap excess queue_wait against baseline, compared to the per-run residual size) -- it may fully explain the residual, or leave its own smaller unexplained remainder, and either outcome should be reported plainly rather than assuming the tidy one.
hypotheses.required_changes: New retroactive analysis script src/real_time_translation/experiments/post_gap_queue_wait.py (console script real-time-translation-exp-post-gap-queue-wait): import _asr_utterance_intervals/_excluded_gaps/GAP_EXCLUSION_THRESHOLD_S from simul_latency_metrics.py and batch_latencies from mt_latency_decomposition.py (no changes to either existing module), tag each batch post-gap/baseline per the join described above, write a small CSV/report comparing the two groups' queue_wait_s per run and the implied AL-residual explanatory share, with unit tests on a synthetic toy event list (a few batches, one injected >10s gap) verifying the tagging logic against a hand-computed expected baseline/post-gap split. Purely retroactive re-analysis of the same 2 already-existing experiment JSONs -- no new Deepgram/LLM calls, no pipeline code change.
hypotheses.result_summary: PARTIALLY CONFIRMED. For both outlier full-lecture runs, batches tagged as the first batch right after an excluded (>10s) gap show a mean queue_wait_s 4.5-5.9x the run's own baseline (llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture: 5/8 gaps resolved, post_gap_mean=7.92s vs baseline_mean=1.35s; _v2_dict: 6/7 gaps resolved, post_gap_mean=6.15s vs baseline_mean=1.26s) -- the predicted direction and rough order of magnitude held, though the formal run's post_gap_mean came out somewhat lower than the GENERATE_HYPOTHESES exploratory pre-check's 7.43-8.47s figure (the pre-check's own note already flagged two low outliers, 2.57s/2.80s, that this formal run's mean necessarily includes). Summing each run's post-gap excess queue_wait (post_gap_queue_wait_s minus that run's baseline mean) against its own ca_al_char_s_gapexcl (cycle 61's unresolved AL residual) gives an explanatory share of 54.9% (first run) and 39.7% (second run) -- so the post-gap MT queueing effect is real and substantial, but accounts for less than half to just over half of the residual, not all of it. A roughly 45-60% remainder of the residual is still unexplained by this mechanism alone; a future hypothesis would need to look elsewhere (e.g. whether settle-time effects propagate forward past just the one post-gap batch, or a different source of inflation entirely) rather than treating this as closing the cycle-61 question.

hypotheses.title: Measure how many batches after a >10s silence gap the elevated MT queue-wait (h-mt-queue-wait-post-gap-residual) persists, to see if propagation beyond just the first post-gap batch explains more of the cycle-61 AL residual
hypotheses.description: h-mt-queue-wait-post-gap-residual (cycle 63 tested) confirmed post-gap batches carry 4.5-5.9x elevated queue_wait_s vs. each run's baseline, but that effect alone only explains 54.9%/39.7% of the two outlier runs' cycle-61 ca_al_char_s_gapexcl residual -- its own result_summary explicitly flags that the remaining ~45-60% could come from the excess propagating forward into the settle times of batches AFTER the first post-gap one, a mechanism post_gap_queue_wait.py's _tag_post_gap_batches() does not measure (it tags only the single nearest-batch-to-gap-end as 'post-gap', everything else as 'baseline', with no notion of a second or third batch still carrying excess queue_wait as the backlog drains). This hypothesis extends that same retroactive analysis to batches at offset 1, 2, 3... after each gap (not just offset 0) to find how many batches it takes for queue_wait_s to return to baseline, and whether summing the excess across all elevated offsets closes more of the residual than the single-batch version did.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expect queue_wait_s to decay from the offset-0 elevation (4.5-5.9x baseline) back toward baseline over a small number of subsequent batches (plausibly 1-3, given each run's baseline batch cadence), not drop to baseline instantly at offset 1 -- a pure single-batch effect would mean h-mt-queue-wait-post-gap-residual's unexplained remainder comes from somewhere else entirely, while a multi-batch decay would mean this hypothesis's wider accounting closes a meaningfully larger share of the residual than that hypothesis's 39.7-54.9%. Either outcome is informative and should be reported as found, not assumed.
hypotheses.required_changes: Extend src/real_time_translation/experiments/post_gap_queue_wait.py's tagging (or add a new retroactive script reusing its _tag_post_gap_batches/batch_latencies imports) to tag each batch by its integer offset from the nearest preceding excluded gap (0, 1, 2, ... up to some small cap, everything else remains 'baseline'), report mean queue_wait_s per offset per run, and recompute explanatory_share_of_gapexcl_al summing excess queue_wait across all offsets found to be elevated (not just offset 0) against the same ca_al_char_s_gapexcl denominator. Add unit tests on a synthetic toy event list covering a multi-batch decay pattern. Purely retroactive re-analysis of the same 2 existing experiment JSONs already used by h-mt-queue-wait-post-gap-residual -- no new Deepgram/LLM calls, no pipeline code change.
hypotheses.result_summary: CONFIRMED (persistence beyond offset 0 is real and materially raises the explanatory share). For both cycle-61/62 outlier full-lecture runs, elevated queue_wait_s does NOT drop back to baseline immediately at the batch after the tagged post-gap anchor: llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture decays over offsets 0/1/2 (7.92s/5.76s/3.83s vs. baseline 1.30s, n=5/2/1) before offset 3 would have fallen back to baseline; llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict decays over offsets 0/1 (6.15s/6.57s vs. baseline 1.21s, n=6/2) before offset 2 falls back. Summing excess queue_wait across all elevated offsets (not just offset 0) raises the explanatory share of each run's own cycle-61 ca_al_char_s_gapexcl residual from h-mt-queue-wait-post-gap-residual's single-batch figures (54.9%/39.7%) to 74.6%/54.7% -- closing most but still not all of the residual (a 25-45% remainder is still unexplained by this mechanism). Caveat: the per-offset sample sizes thin out fast (n=1-2 at the highest elevated offset in both runs), so the exact decay length (2 vs 3 batches) is noisier than the overall direction/magnitude of the effect; this should be read as 'the effect clearly spans multiple batches, not just one' rather than a precise batch-count. Incidental finding: running the generic experiments/*.json glob (not restricted to the 2 cycle-61 outlier runs) surfaced 2 more runs with excluded gaps -- full_llm2025_zenhan_gemini3flash_s0 (23.7%) and full_llm2025_zenhan_gpt54mini_s0 (30.3%) -- with smaller explanatory shares and shorter 1-2-offset decays; these were not part of cycle-61's original residual question (that was specific to the 2 outlier full-lecture runs) so are reported here as additional supporting evidence for the same qualitative persistence effect, not as closing a different residual.

hypotheses.title: Test whether a dependency-free EN verb-position proxy for EN->JA reordering burden correlates with per-utterance MT latency or fidelity (grounded in doi2024-enja-si-word-order, previously uncited)
hypotheses.description: doi2024-enja-si-word-order documents that English-Japanese simultaneous interpretation is unusually burdened by word-order divergence: English SVO vs. Japanese SOV means the Japanese predicate/verb lands clause-finally, so an incremental interpreter often must wait for the English verb before committing the Japanese sentence. This repo's LLM batch translator commits full utterances/batches rather than word-by-word, so the effect (if any) would show up as a correlation between how late the main verb appears in the English source and this utterance's MT latency/fidelity, not as an incremental-policy failure. This hypothesis is purely retroactive: only is_utterance_end=True translation_complete events are used, because cycle-17's reflections.md finding (original_text is NOT reliably cumulative across mid-utterance batch transitions, only 76% prefix-nested) does not apply to the is_utterance_end=True commit path -- pipeline.py's utterance-end branch (around _emit_batch_result's acc_source handling, ~pipeline.py:571-594) sets original_text to the utterance's full accumulated source text and translated_text to the full committed translation, which is the known-clean case, not the known-unreliable one. No NLP library (spacy/nltk/etc.) is in pyproject.toml's dependencies, so the verb-position proxy must be a dependency-free heuristic (e.g. a small closed-class list of common English modal/auxiliary + finite-verb suffix patterns to locate the likely main verb token index, normalized by sentence token count) -- this is explicitly a coarse proxy, not a validated POS tagger, and the write-up must say so plainly rather than overstating its precision.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expect utterances whose proxy verb-position lands later in the English sentence (heavier predicted reordering burden) to show mildly elevated per-utterance queue_wait_s/stream_duration_s (joined from mt_latency_decomposition.py's existing per-batch output, aggregated to each utterance's final committing batch) and/or lower recorded fidelity scores already in results.csv -- but since this pipeline commits whole utterances rather than translating incrementally word-by-word, the expected effect size is small or possibly undetectable given the heuristic's coarseness; report whichever outcome (including null) the data actually shows rather than forcing a positive finding.
hypotheses.required_changes: New retroactive analysis script under src/real_time_translation/experiments/ (e.g. word_order_reordering_proxy.py) that: (1) reuses mt_latency_decomposition.batch_latencies() for per-batch queue_wait_s/stream_duration_s, (2) filters to is_utterance_end=True translation_complete events across all experiments/*.json with results.events, (3) computes the dependency-free verb-position proxy on each utterance's original_text, (4) correlates the proxy against queue_wait_s/stream_duration_s and against results.csv's per-run fidelity/chrF columns where resolvable, reporting Pearson/Spearman and an honest null-result path if correlation is weak. No live Deepgram/LLM calls, no pipeline code changes. Add unit tests for the proxy heuristic on a handful of hand-picked English sentences with known verb positions.
experiment_ids: retroactive: all experiments/*.json with a results.events list (139 files, via experiments/word_order_reordering_proxy.csv)
hypotheses.result_summary: INCONCLUSIVE / LARGELY NULL (honest null result, not a confound). Ran word_order_reordering_proxy.py over all 139 experiments/*.json files: 5087 is_utterance_end=True utterances, verb_position_ratio resolved for 2586 of them (resolution_rate=50.8% -- about half of spoken-lecture sentences have no closed-class auxiliary/modal/copula token at all, e.g. simple-present constructions, so the heuristic is honestly silent on those rather than guessing). Mean verb_position_ratio=0.376 (the proxy verb tends to land in the first 40% of the sentence on average, consistent with English's SV-early structure). MAIN RESULT (well-powered, n=2586): verb_position_ratio vs stream_duration_s shows essentially no correlation (pearson_r=0.049, spearman_r=0.057) -- i.e. a later-landing English verb (heavier predicted reordering burden per doi2024-enja-si-word-order) does NOT measurably slow down how long the LLM takes to stream out the Japanese translation once it starts. This matches the predicted_effect's null branch: this pipeline commits/translates the whole accumulated utterance as a single LLM call regardless of internal clause structure, unlike an incremental word-by-word SI policy where a late verb would directly stall the next commit decision -- so the reordering-burden mechanism doi2024-enja-si-word-order describes for human/incremental SI does not carry over to this batch-translation architecture, at least not via stream_duration_s. SECONDARY RESULT (underpowered, n=157, do not over-read): verb_position_ratio vs queue_wait_s gives pearson_r=-0.055 and spearman_r=+0.305 -- inconsistent in sign between the two correlation measures at this sample size, and n=157 is only the utterances where BOTH the proxy AND queue_wait_s happen to resolve (queue_wait_s itself only resolves for 711/5087=14% of utterance-end batches corpus-wide, a known content_ready-lookup limitation carried over unchanged from h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition, and that 14% intersects with the proxy's own 50.8% resolution less than independence alone would predict -- 157 observed vs ~362 expected if independent -- suggesting some structural overlap between which utterances get which kind of missing data, not investigated further here since it is not this hypothesis's question). This secondary number should be read as 'no usable signal at this sample size', not as evidence of a reversed or queue-wait-specific effect.
