CONCLUSION: the EN->JA word-order reordering-burden mechanism from doi2024-enja-si-word-order, while real for human/incremental interpretation, does not detectably affect this pipeline's per-utterance MT latency -- a genuinely informative null result for a previously-uncited paper, not a confound or implementation bug. No further experiments on this specific question are warranted; doi2024-enja-si-word-order may still be relevant to *translation quality/naturalness* (not latency), which this hypothesis did not test and is a possible future angle.

hypotheses.title: Does requesting explicit reasoning BEFORE the numeric score reduce translation_fidelity_judge()'s per-call scoring noise? (grounded in rubriceval2603, previously uncited)
hypotheses.description: rubriceval2603 (RubricEval) reports that explicit reasoning (chain-of-thought) before the verdict improves LLM-judge accuracy on rubric-item grading and, combined with rubric-level (vs checklist-level) grading, reduces inter-judge variance; ruverbench2606 independently confirms, in a different domain, that judge noise under rubric-item verification is a general phenomenon and that majority voting/repeat-averaging has diminishing returns -- both previously uncited by any hypothesis (see papers.json's own cross_reference_check_cycle56 notes on both entries, which flagged this exact gap but left it for GENERATE_HYPOTHESES). Verified directly against the actual code before writing this (translation_fidelity_judge.py:40-63, and judge_schematic_adherence_replay.py:64-87): every judge prompt variant in this codebase requests its numeric score field(s) with no preceding free-text rationale -- the base judge asks for {"score": ..., "dropped_or_distorted": ..., "notes": ...} (score first, a one-sentence 'notes' field last, not a reasoning pass before scoring), and the decomposed-rubric variant asks for the 4 named sub-criteria then the holistic "score" last -- still no free-text reasoning field at all, let alone one preceding a numeric field. Reasoning-before-score, as RubricEval frames it, has never actually been tried here. Separately, this hypothesis deliberately improves on a known limitation of cycle 19-21's existing noise-floor baseline (within_group_noise_stdev 3.40 / 8.81 on the two source clips, see experiments/judge_noise_power_analysis_summary.json): that baseline's judge() calls were made once per REPEATS-translation-run (confirmed by reading soft_anchor_gate_recalibrated_replay.py's repeat loop, ~line 144-152: judge() is called once per each of the 2 separately-*generated* translation repeats), so it conflates translation-generation stochasticity with judge-scoring stochasticity. This hypothesis instead fixes ONE translation text per sampled span x condition (repeats[0]'s final cumulative text, same convention as judge_schematic_adherence_replay.py) and calls judge() K=2 times on that exact same fixed (source, translation) pair for each of two prompt variants, isolating pure judge-scoring noise from translation noise for the first time in this codebase.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: If RubricEval's reasoning-before-score finding generalizes to this fact-retention judging task, the reasoning-first variant's within-group (same fixed text, repeated judge calls) score stdev should be measurably lower than the current score-first variant's, on the same sampled zero-effect span x condition points. This is a single low-power check (K=2 judge-repeats per point, matching this repo's existing REPEATS=2 convention, ~34 sampled groups) -- report an honest null if the two variants' noise is statistically indistinguishable or the difference is within what K=2 can resolve, rather than overstating a small difference as confirmed (per ANALYZE_RESULTS's noise-floor caution).
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/judge_reasoning_order_replay.py that: (1) loads experiments/20260921_h_soft_anchor_gate_recalibrated_noisefloor_replay.json's by_source, restricted to zero-effect spans (gated_batch_indices == []) sampled at span_index % 4 == 0 (matching judge_schematic_adherence_replay.py's stride-sampling convention, scaled to bound cost at ~34 span x condition groups across both source clips' soft_anchor_replay/gated_soft_anchor conditions); (2) for each sampled group, takes repeats[0]'s last_cumulative_text (reusing results_io.last_cumulative_text) as ONE fixed translation text -- the translation is NOT regenerated; (3) calls the EXISTING unmodified translation_fidelity_judge.judge() K=2 times on that fixed (source_full, translation) pair for the current score-first prompt, and a NEW reasoning-first prompt variant (defined locally in the new script, e.g. {"reasoning": <2-3 sentence free-text analysis>, "dropped_or_distorted": [...], "score": <int 0-100>}, reasoning requested first in the schema) K=2 times on the identical fixed pair; (4) computes each group's within-group stdev per variant and the mean within-group stdev across groups per variant (reusing stats.stdev()), reporting both variants side by side plus a paired per-group stdev comparison. Does NOT modify translation_fidelity_judge.py itself -- the reasoning-first prompt stays a replay-only variant until/unless this hypothesis confirms a real effect worth adopting into production. No live Deepgram calls, no pipeline/production code changes. Zero new translation generation (pure replay of already-recorded text); only new spend is the judge() calls themselves.
hypotheses.result_summary: CONTRADICTED (clean, same-magnitude-as-predicted but opposite-direction effect). On 34 sampled zero-effect span x condition groups, each judged K=2 times with the SAME fixed, already-recorded translation text for both prompt variants (so translation-generation stochasticity is fully controlled out -- confirmed by inspecting the raw rows: 136/136 calls parsed cleanly, no dropped points), reasoning-first within_group_noise_stdev=7.74 is roughly 2.4x score-first's 3.27 (variance ratio ~5.6x). Paired per-group delta (reasoning_first_stdev - score_first_stdev) has mean +1.66 and is positive (reasoning-first noisier) for the clear majority of groups with any delta at all, dominated by a handful of large positive outliers: span 28/soft_anchor_replay went from a perfectly-reproduced [60,60] under score-first to [95,50] under reasoning-first on the IDENTICAL text; span 40/gated_soft_anchor went from [75,70] to [100,60]. This is the opposite of rubriceval2603's finding that explicit reasoning before the verdict reduces inter-judge variance. Plausible mechanism (not confirmed, offered as a hypothesis for why this task differs from RubricEval's): RubricEval's reasoning step is a constrained per-rubric-item satisfied/not-satisfied check, whereas this judge's reasoning field is open-ended free text about overall content retention -- an unconstrained narrative can commit to a different interpretive framing each call (e.g. 'basically preserved the gist' vs 'actually lost the key number'), and the final score then follows whichever framing that call's reasoning happened to generate, amplifying rather than damping call-to-call variance. A second, unconfirmed, non-exclusive explanation: simply moving the score token later in the completion (after a longer free-text span) could itself add generation-position instability, independent of the reasoning content's substance -- this experiment cannot distinguish the two mechanisms, only that the net effect of the reordering is more noise, not less. Conclusion: do NOT adopt a reasoning-first prompt into translation_fidelity_judge.py's production judge based on this result; RubricEval's finding does not generalize as-is to this open-ended fact-retention scoring task. Caveat: K=2 per point is this repo's standard REPEATS convention but is still a single low-power check per group -- the aggregate within_group_noise_stdev comparison (34 groups each) is the more reliable number here than any individual group's delta, and that aggregate comparison is what actually drives this conclusion, not the outliers alone.

hypotheses.title: Does translation_fidelity_judge()'s per-call noise shrink with K judge-repeats the way plain i.i.d. scaling predicts, or does it converge faster/slower (grounded in ruverbench2606, same paper already cited for reasoning-order, but this specific claim untested)?
hypotheses.description: ruverbench2606 reports that majority voting / repeat-averaging reduces LLM-judge noise but with diminishing returns as more repeat votes are added. Cycle 65's reflections.md explicitly flagged this specific claim as not yet tested here, distinct from the reasoning-order claim of the same paper already tested in h-judge-reasoning-before-score-noise. This repo's own judge-noise work (cycles 19-22, cycle 65) has only ever used K=2 judge-repeats per point (this repo's standard REPEATS convention) and has never measured how the noise of the *mean* estimator actually changes as more repeats are added past 2. Verified against the code before writing this: translation_fidelity_judge.judge() (translation_fidelity_judge.py:40-63) takes a single (source, translation) pair and returns one score per call with no internal repeat/aggregation logic of its own -- any multi-repeat averaging is done by the caller (as cycle 65's judge_reasoning_order_replay.py already does for K=2), so raising K is purely a caller-side change, not a judge-prompt change. This hypothesis reuses cycle 65's fixed-translation-text design exactly (same source JSON experiments/20260921_h_soft_anchor_gate_recalibrated_noisefloor_replay.json, same 34 zero-effect span x condition groups sampled at span_index %% 4 == 0, same production score_first prompt only -- NOT the reasoning_first variant, since cycle 65 showed that one is strictly worse and not a candidate for production) but raises K from 2 to 5 judge-repeats per group, then empirically checks whether the realized reduction in the mean estimator's variance as K' grows from 1 to 5 tracks the naive i.i.d. prediction (variance of mean of K' draws = single-draw variance / K', estimated per-group from that group's own 5-draw sample variance) or diverges from it. Diverging slower-than-1/K' would mean per-group judge draws are positively correlated (e.g. the model anchors near its own prior answer), making additional repeats less useful than the simple model assumes; diverging faster would mean the opposite.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Per ruverbench2606, expect noise to decrease as K grows but with diminishing marginal benefit -- the open, previously-untested question for this repo is whether the empirical mean-of-K' variance (computed directly from each group's 5 actual judge draws, via all size-K' subsets of each group's 5 draws, K'=1..5) tracks the naive 1/K' scaling from K'=1 reasonably closely, or whether it flattens out faster (repeats become useless sooner than 1/K' implies, meaning this repo's current REPEATS=2 convention is already capturing most of the achievable benefit and raising it further would not be worth the added judge-call cost) or slower (more repeats would meaningfully keep helping, an actionable finding for a future budget-policy proposal). Single K_MAX=5 per group is still a modest-power check (same spirit as cycles 19-22's own low-power caveats) -- report the comparison honestly rather than overstating a small gap between empirical and theoretical curves as a confirmed mechanism.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/judge_repeat_diminishing_returns.py that: (1) reuses judge_reasoning_order_replay.py's _sampled_groups()/score_first prompt and fixed-translation-text convention exactly (same source JSON, same 34 groups, same score_first-only prompt copied in, since the existing module isn't designed to be imported as a library function for a different K -- confirmed by reading it: _judge_once/_sampled_groups have no K parameter); (2) for each sampled group, calls judge() K_MAX=5 times (not 2) on the identical fixed (source_full, translation) pair, recording all 5 raw scores (170 total new judge calls across 34 groups); (3) for each group, computes, for every K' in 1..5, the empirical variance of the mean across all C(5, K') same-size subsets of that group's 5 draws (itertools.combinations, no new live calls needed since all subsets are reused from the same 5 already-collected draws); (4) averages each K''s subset-mean-variance across all 34 groups to get one empirical curve point per K', and separately computes the naive theoretical prediction (each group's own 5-draw sample variance divided by K', averaged the same way) as the baseline i.i.d. comparison curve; (5) reports both curves side by side plus their ratio at each K', so a ratio near 1.0 at every K' supports plain i.i.d. scaling (ruverbench2606's 'diminishing returns' is then just ordinary 1/sqrt(K) statistics, not a repo-specific extra effect) while a ratio that grows with K signals faster-than-predicted flattening (positive correlation between repeats). Does NOT modify translation_fidelity_judge.py or any production code -- replay-only, same as h-judge-reasoning-before-score-noise. Zero new Deepgram spend, zero new translation generation; only new spend is the extra judge() calls (170 total vs cycle 65's 136, similar per-call rate).
hypotheses.result_summary: INCONCLUSIVE -- design flaw caught during ANALYZE_RESULTS before being reported as a finding (same spirit as cycle 12's config-diff confound and cycle 19-21's noise-floor caveats). 170/170 live gemini-3.1-flash-lite judge calls parsed cleanly (34 zero-effect span x condition groups x K_MAX=5 fixed-text repeats each, identical sampling/prompt to h-judge-reasoning-before-score-noise). The raw empirical_over_theoretical_ratio curve (1.0, 0.667, 0.444, 0.25 at K'=1..4, computed as: empirical = variance of the mean across all C(5,K') subsets drawn WITHOUT replacement from each group's fixed 5 real draws; theoretical = each group's own 5-draw sample variance / K', the naive i.i.d.-with-replacement prediction) looked, at first glance, like strong evidence that repeated judge calls on the identical input are positively correlated (noise shrinks faster than naive 1/K scaling predicts, i.e. repeats help MORE than naively assumed). Before writing that up as a finding, ran a synthetic control: 34 groups x 5 draws from a TRUE i.i.d. Gaussian(50,10) generator (random.seed(42), zero real correlation by construction) through the IDENTICAL analysis code. The synthetic curve was numerically IDENTICAL (1.0, 0.667, 0.444, 0.25) to the real-data curve. This proves the ratio-shrinking-below-1.0 pattern is a deterministic artifact of exhaustively enumerating subsets without replacement from one small FIXED finite sample (a finite-population-correction effect that occurs regardless of whether the underlying process is correlated or not), not evidence about this repo's actual judge-call correlation structure. See the experiment JSON's `synthetic_control_check` key for the full derivation and numbers. Conclusion: the hypothesis's actual question (does translation_fidelity_judge() noise reduction, as repeat count K grows, track naive 1/K i.i.d. scaling or diverge from it due to real correlation between repeated calls on the same input) remains UNTESTED as of this cycle -- this experiment's method cannot answer it, by construction, no matter what data it's run on. A valid test would need genuinely independent per-K replicate BATCHES (e.g. actually drawing fresh K=2, K=3, K=4, K=5 samples as separate live judge-call sets, not combinatorially subsetting one fixed K=5 batch) rather than exhaustive subset enumeration of a single small fixed sample. Not re-run this cycle (depth-over-breadth; a corrected redesign is noted as a candidate for a future cycle in reflections.md rather than immediately re-attempted). As a side observation (not the hypothesis's main question, and not independently verified against a noise floor so should not be over-read): the K=1 mean variance across the 34 groups (15.15, i.e. stdev~3.89) is in the same rough order of magnitude as cycle 65's score_first within_group_noise_stdev=3.27 (variance~10.7) measured on an overlapping sample of the same source data, which is at least a sane sanity check that nothing is badly broken in the raw judge-call pipeline itself.

hypotheses.title: Corrected redesign of h-judge-repeat-count-diminishing-returns: using genuinely independent replicate batches (not combinatorial subsetting of one fixed 5-draw sample), does translation_fidelity_judge() noise actually shrink with K the way plain i.i.d. scaling predicts?
hypotheses.description: Cycle 66's h-judge-repeat-count-diminishing-returns tried to answer this same ruverbench2606 claim (majority voting / repeat-averaging reduces LLM-judge noise with diminishing returns) by drawing exactly 5 judge() calls per group and then examining the empirical variance of the mean across every combinatorial subset (without replacement) of that single fixed 5-draw sample, for K'=1..5. That method was caught as invalid during ANALYZE_RESULTS (see result_summary on h-judge-repeat-count-diminishing-returns and reflections.md's cycle-66 entry, now also written into PLAYBOOK.md's ANALYZE_RESULTS section): a synthetic i.i.d. control run through the identical analysis code reproduced the exact same empirical/theoretical ratio curve (1.0, 0.667, 0.444, 0.25), proving the shrinkage is a deterministic finite-population-correction artifact of exhaustive without-replacement subsetting of one small fixed sample, not evidence about real judge-call correlation. The underlying research question (does translation_fidelity_judge()'s repeated-call noise on an identical fixed (source, translation) pair track naive 1/K i.i.d. variance scaling, or deviate from it because of positive/negative correlation between repeated calls) therefore remains genuinely untested. Cycle 66's own reflections.md explicitly flagged 'a corrected redesign (independent per-K replicate batches rather than combinatorial subsetting)' as the concrete next step, which this hypothesis implements. Design: reuse the identical 34 zero-effect span x condition groups, fixed (source_full, translation) pairs, and production score_first judge prompt from h-judge-repeat-count-diminishing-returns's _sampled_groups() (same source JSON experiments/20260921_h_soft_anchor_gate_recalibrated_noisefloor_replay.json, same span_index %% 4 == 0 stride, same two conditions soft_anchor_replay / gated_soft_anchor) -- but instead of one fixed 5-draw sample per group, draw B=5 INDEPENDENT batches per group, each batch containing K_MAX=5 fresh judge() calls on the identical pair (no call reused across batches or across groups). For each K' in 1..5, take the mean of the first K' elements of each of the 5 independent batches -- since each batch's 5 elements are themselves i.i.d. draws, the first-K'-elements mean of a given batch is a valid i.i.d.-mean-of-K' statistic, and because the 5 batches are drawn fully independently of each other, the 5 resulting K'-means ARE genuinely independent replicates of that statistic (unlike cycle 66's combinatorial subsets of one batch, which overlap and are therefore correlated by construction). This gives an unbiased empirical estimate of Var(mean of K' draws) for every K', fixing the exact flaw cycle 66 found, while reusing the same groups/prompt/source data for direct comparability and only costing 34 groups x 5 batches x 5 calls = 850 new judge calls (vs cycle 66's 170), still zero new Deepgram spend and zero new translation generation (same fixed, already-recorded source/translation text, only new judge() calls).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: If translation_fidelity_judge()'s repeated calls on an identical input are genuinely i.i.d. (no anchoring/memory effect across calls), the empirical Var(mean of K') computed from the 5 independent batches should track the theoretical sigma_hat^2/K' prediction (sigma_hat^2 estimated by pooling all 25 draws per group) reasonably closely at every K', within the sampling noise expected from only 5 independent replicates per K' (this is still a modest-power check -- same honesty caveat as cycles 19-22's own noise-floor work -- so a small empirical/theoretical ratio deviation at a single K' should not be over-read; look at whether the ratio trends consistently away from 1.0 as K' grows, not just its value at one K'). A ratio that consistently exceeds 1.0 as K' grows would mean repeats are positively correlated (each repeat call anchors near a similar score, so added repeats help less than naive 1/K scaling assumes) -- consistent with ruverbench2606's qualitative 'diminishing returns beyond naive 1/K' framing, but this time from a design that can actually support that conclusion. A ratio that stays near 1.0 throughout would mean this repo's REPEATS convention is already getting the full naive-expected benefit from added repeats, and ruverbench2606's diminishing-returns claim (measured in a different domain, rubric verification, not translation fidelity scoring) does not transfer here. As an internal validity check (per the new PLAYBOOK.md rule this cycle's predecessor added), also re-run cycle 66's exact synthetic-i.i.d.-control procedure through this corrected analysis code with fabricated Gaussian data -- it should NOT reproduce a deterministic shrinking curve this time, confirming the fix actually removed the artifact rather than just changing its shape.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/judge_repeat_independent_batches.py that: (1) imports _sampled_groups() from judge_repeat_diminishing_returns.py unchanged (same 34-group sampling, verified by inspection to need no K-related parameters) rather than re-implementing it; (2) for each sampled group, draws B=5 independent batches, each calling judge_repeat_diminishing_returns._judge_once(source_full, translation) K_MAX=5 times fresh (25 total judge calls per group, 850 across 34 groups) -- critically, each batch's 5 calls and each of the 5 batches must be drawn with no reuse of any score across batches (do not reuse cycle 66's existing 170 stored scores at all; this hypothesis's entire point is that those scores came from one non-independent batch); (3) for each K' in 1..5 and each of the 5 batches, computes the mean of that batch's first K' scores; (4) computes the empirical Var(mean of K') per group as the sample variance (ddof=1) across those 5 batch-means; (5) estimates sigma_hat^2 per group by pooling all 25 collected scores for that group (sample variance), and computes the theoretical prediction sigma_hat^2/K'; (6) averages both the empirical and theoretical values across all groups per K' (same aggregation style as cycle 66's script) and reports their ratio, plus the per-group raw data so the ratio's own uncertainty (only 5 independent replicates per K' per group) is visible in the output JSON; (7) re-runs cycle 66's exact synthetic-i.i.d.-control check (fabricated Gaussian(50,10) data, same B=5/K_MAX=5 structure, same analysis code) as a built-in sanity gate before any real-data conclusion is drawn, writing both the real-data and synthetic-control curves into the output JSON for direct side-by-side comparison. Does NOT modify translation_fidelity_judge.py or any production code -- replay-only, same as its predecessor. Zero new Deepgram spend, zero new translation generation; only new spend is 850 new gemini-3.1-flash-lite judge() calls (vs cycle 66's 170), estimated by scaling cycle 66's measured $0.07/170-call rate (~$0.00041/call) to 850 calls.

hypotheses.title: Formalize the already-flagged 'anchoring reduces repeat-to-repeat NE variance, not just mean NE' observation into a real within-span-vs-between-span variance decomposition, purely retroactive over two already-recorded replay JSONs
hypotheses.description: h-hard-prefix-lock-continuation's result_summary noted in passing that baseline_replay showed visibly higher repeat-to-repeat NE variance than soft_anchor_replay/hard_lock (e.g. span 13: 1.0 vs 1.586 across its 2 repeats) and flagged it as 'a secondary finding worth a future hypothesis'. h-soft-anchor-generalization-guest-talk's result_summary independently re-observed the same pattern on a second, larger clip ('baseline hit NE=0 in only 9/166 (5%) repeat-runs vs soft_anchor's 123/166 (74%) -- consistent with the original clip's finding that anchoring reduces run-to-run flicker variance, not just its mean') but, like the first, did not formalize this into a dedicated analysis -- both treated it as an aside while focused on their own primary mean-NE question. Neither hypothesis actually decomposed the variance or quantified the effect; this one does, reusing the exact between-vs-within decomposition methodology already established and committed in judge_noise_power_analysis.py's _decompose_zero_effect_variance() (cycle 21: pool raw repeat values across spans only AFTER averaging within-span variance, not before -- the cycle-19/20 near-miss this repo's own playbook now warns against conflating). Both source replay JSONs already store a 'condition_ne' list of exactly REPEATS=2 raw NE values per span per condition (verified by reading experiments/20260919_h_hard_prefix_lock_replay.json and experiments/20260919_h_soft_anchor_generalization_guest_talk.json directly) -- no re-translation, no new judge() calls, no live API access of any kind is needed; this is pure arithmetic over numbers already on disk.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expect mean within-span repeat variance of NE to be materially lower for soft_anchor_replay than for baseline_replay on both clips (hard_lock excluded from the variance comparison -- its condition_ne is [0.0, 0.0] in every span by construction, zero variance trivially and uninformatively, exactly as h-hard-prefix-lock-continuation's own result_summary already concluded for its mean). This would upgrade 'anchoring also reduces run-to-run unpredictability' from a passing observation in two unrelated result_summary sections to a quantified, decomposed finding -- useful supporting evidence for promoting anchor_continuation_translation out of experimental status (same recommendation both source hypotheses already made on mean-NE grounds alone). A null or reversed result (soft_anchor variance >= baseline variance once properly decomposed) would mean the two prior passing mentions were themselves an artifact of only 2 repeats per span and should be retracted/qualified in a future reflections.md note rather than repeated as received wisdom.
hypotheses.required_changes: New analysis script src/real_time_translation/experiments/soft_anchor_repeat_variance_decomposition.py: (1) load both experiments/20260919_h_hard_prefix_lock_replay.json and experiments/20260919_h_soft_anchor_generalization_guest_talk.json; (2) for each file, for each span, for each condition present (baseline_replay/soft_anchor_replay in both files, hard_lock only in the first), read condition_ne[condition] (a list of exactly 2 raw floats per span when defined -- skip spans where fewer than 2 non-null values exist, same num_spans_with_defined_ne-style filtering each source script already applies); (3) compute each span's own within-span sample variance (ddof=1, i.e. single pairwise squared difference over 1 for the n=2 case) per condition; (4) average those within-span variances across all usable spans per condition per clip (this is the 'within-group' step of judge_noise_power_analysis.py's established decomposition -- average variances, never pool raw values across spans first); (5) separately compute each condition's between-span variance (variance of each span's own 2-repeat mean NE, across spans) for comparison/context, making the within-vs-between distinction explicit in the output exactly as cycle 21 did for judge noise; (6) report both per-clip and pooled-across-both-clips numbers, plus simple descriptive stats (min/max/median within-span variance per condition) so a single misleading mean doesn't hide a shift in distribution shape. No pipeline.py/llm_translator.py changes, no new translate_stream or judge() calls of any kind -- pure Python arithmetic over two files already on disk. Follows this repo's replay/analysis-script precedent (no results.csv row, per the convention already established by flicker_metrics.py and prefix_lock_replay.py for non-chrF/latency-comparable analyses).
hypotheses.result_summary: Ran soft_anchor_repeat_variance_decomposition.py over both existing replay JSONs (no live API calls). RESULT IS MIXED, more interesting than the prediction: on the original (cleaner) clip, soft_anchor_replay's mean within-span repeat variance is dramatically lower than baseline_replay's (0.00054 vs 0.0216, ~40x) -- confirms h-hard-prefix-lock-continuation's passing observation cleanly. But on the guest-talk (disfluent) clip, the MEAN within-span variance is actually HIGHER for soft_anchor_replay than baseline_replay (0.1026 vs 0.0399) -- the opposite of h-soft-anchor-generalization-guest-talk's passing claim that '9/166 vs 123/166 NE=0 hits' meant anchoring reduces variance there too. Decomposing further: the MEDIAN within-span variance is still lower for soft_anchor on this clip (0.0 vs 0.0023, consistent with the typical span truly being more stable under anchoring, matching the passing observation), but the MEAN is entirely dominated by one extreme outlier, span 73 (source: 'I traditional IO trained methods. So it's good... it's very very expensive.'): soft_anchor_replay's two repeats were NE=0.0 and NE=3.76 -- repeat 0 produced a correct full translation, repeat 1 instead output ONLY the tail clause ('非常にコストがかかるという点です。', 'it's very expensive', dropping the entire preceding sentence about IO-trained methods and its disadvantages) -- a previously-undetected intermittent catastrophic-truncation failure mode in soft_anchor_replay, distinct from the generalization hypothesis's already-documented hallucination-under-disfluency failure mode (span 69). This went completely undetected by the existing fidelity evaluation because translation_fidelity_judge.judge() is only called once per condition per span, on repeats[0] (per ANALYZE_RESULTS's own established noise-floor caveat from cycle 19) -- repeats[0] for span 73 happened to be the good, complete translation, so judge_scores shows a clean 100/no-drops for soft_anchor_replay on this exact span despite repeat 1's severe truncation existing right next to it in the same JSON. A second, smaller outlier (span 34, both repeats are full retranslation variants with real but more ordinary wording differences, not a truncation) is the next-largest contributor. Between-span variance (how much average NE differs span-to-span) decreases under anchoring on BOTH clips (original: 0.287->0.080; guest-talk: 0.221->0.069), a separate, more unambiguous stability benefit distinct from the mixed within-span-repeat-variance picture. CONCLUSION: the two prior hypotheses' passing 'anchoring also reduces run-to-run variance' claims are correct on typical-case/median grounds on both clips and on between-span grounds, but ONE quantified exception was found that neither caught: an intermittent, judge()-invisible catastrophic truncation in soft_anchor_replay, concentrated (so far, n=1 observed instance in 98 total spans across both clips) in longer/more complex source sentences on disfluent speech. Not large enough-n to estimate a real rate, but real and specific enough to flag before anchor_continuation_translation is promoted out of experimental status: RECOMMEND a follow-up hypothesis that (a) checks all repeats (not just repeats[0]) for a length/overlap sanity check against the span's own cumulative source text (e.g. flag any translation repeat under some fraction of the OTHER same-span-same-condition repeat's character length) as a cheap, judge-free truncation detector, and (b) if the rate holds up under more spans, consider a server-side guard against anchored output silently collapsing to a short tail fragment. Per this repo's established replay/analysis-script precedent, no results.csv row added.

hypotheses.title: Build a cheap, judge()-free length/overlap sanity check that flags intermittent catastrophic truncation in soft_anchor_replay, directly following up on cycle 70's single discovered instance (span 73)
hypotheses.description: h-soft-anchor-repeat-variance-decomposition's result_summary (cycle 70, 2026-10-22) found that soft_anchor_replay's MEAN within-span repeat variance on the guest-talk clip is inflated above baseline by exactly one outlier span (73): repeat 0 produced a correct full translation, repeat 1 instead output only the tail clause, dropping an entire preceding sentence -- a previously-undetected intermittent catastrophic-truncation failure mode, invisible to translation_fidelity_judge.judge() because judge() is only ever called on repeats[0] (ANALYZE_RESULTS's own established cycle-19 caveat), and repeats[0] for span 73 happened to be the clean repeat. That result_summary explicitly recommended (a) a length/overlap sanity check against each span's own cumulative source text, run over ALL repeats (not just repeats[0]), as a cheap judge-free truncation detector, and (b) if the rate holds up under more spans, consider a server-side guard. This hypothesis implements recommendation (a) only, purely retroactively, as a necessary first step before (b) can even be evaluated (currently n=1 observed instance across 98 total spans, nowhere near enough to estimate a real rate or justify a production guard).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expect the detector to recover span 73's already-known soft_anchor_replay repeat-1 truncation as a clear flag (sanity check: if it doesn't, the detector's threshold/logic is wrong, not that the known case was a fluke). The open empirical question is whether span 73 is truly the only instance across all 98 spans x repeats x conditions in both source JSONs, or whether the same judge()-repeats[0]-only blind spot hid additional unflagged truncations in baseline_replay/hard_lock as well (hard_lock seems structurally immune by construction -- frozen prefix can't be rewritten -- but this should be verified empirically, not assumed, per this playbook's own repeated 'verify against actual data, don't reason abstractly' pattern). A null result (span 73 confirmed as the only flagged instance everywhere) would mean recommendation (b) (a production guard) is not yet justified by volume and should wait for more spans/clips; finding 2+ more instances would materially raise the priority of (b) before anchor_continuation_translation is promoted out of experimental status.
hypotheses.required_changes: New analysis script src/real_time_translation/experiments/soft_anchor_truncation_detector.py: (1) load the same two source JSONs as h-soft-anchor-repeat-variance-decomposition (experiments/20260919_h_hard_prefix_lock_replay.json, experiments/20260919_h_soft_anchor_generalization_guest_talk.json) -- confirmed by direct inspection to be the only 2 experiment JSONs under experiments/ with a condition_repeats field; (2) for each span, for each condition (baseline_replay/soft_anchor_replay in both files, hard_lock only in the first), read condition_repeats[condition] (a list of repeats, each repeat itself a list of per-batch cumulative_text-style strings -- confirmed by reading experiments/20260919_h_hard_prefix_lock_replay.json directly: condition_repeats[condition][repeat_idx][-1] is that repeat's final cumulative translation for the span); (3) for each span+condition with >=2 repeats, compare each repeat's final-batch text length (character count, matching this repo's existing NE/erasure character-based convention, not word count) against the OTHER repeat(s) of the same span+condition; flag a repeat as a suspected truncation if its length is under a fixed fraction (start with 40%, matching span 73's actual ratio so the detector's threshold is calibrated against the one known real case rather than picked arbitrarily -- report the exact ratio found for span 73 in the script's own output so this choice is auditable) of the longest sibling repeat's length; (4) report, per clip per condition: total span+condition groups checked, number flagged, which span indices were flagged, and each flagged repeat's actual vs sibling length so a human can spot-check for false positives (e.g. a repeat that is genuinely short because the source utterance itself was short, not because of truncation -- cross-check flagged spans' source_full length too, since a short-but-complete repeat of a short source span should not be flagged); (5) confirm span 73 is recovered as expected (recommended sanity check in point 1 above). No pipeline.py/llm_translator.py changes, no new translate_stream or judge() calls -- pure Python string-length arithmetic over data already on disk, zero live API access of any kind. Follows this repo's replay/analysis-script precedent (no results.csv row, per the convention flicker_metrics.py/prefix_lock_replay.py/soft_anchor_repeat_variance_decomposition.py already established for non-chrF/latency-comparable analyses).
hypotheses.result_summary: Ran soft_anchor_truncation_detector.py over the same 2 existing replay JSONs as h-soft-anchor-repeat-variance-decomposition (98 spans total, 15 original_clip + 83 guest_talk_clip, x up to 3 conditions each). No live API calls, no config-diff/confound concern applies (pure arithmetic over fixed numbers already on disk, same precedent as the parent hypothesis). SANITY CHECK PASSED: span 73 (cycle 70's known guest-talk soft_anchor_replay truncation) is correctly recovered -- repeat 1's final text (17 chars, 'non-dekosuto-gakakaru-to-iu-ten-desu', the tail-only fragment) is 22.37% of repeat 0's length (76 chars, the full correct translation), well under the 40% flag threshold (itself calibrated with ~1.8x margin above this exact known case). RESULT: span 73 remains the ONLY flagged instance across all 196 span+condition groups checked (15x3 + 83x2, since hard_lock only exists in the original_clip source) -- 0 additional truncations found in baseline_replay (either clip), hard_lock (confirmed structurally immune by construction, 0/15, as predicted), or soft_anchor_replay on the original_clip. This answers the predicted_effect's open empirical question: n=1 is confirmed as the true count (not an artifact of judge()'s repeats[0]-only blind spot hiding more instances elsewhere) across the full 98-span sample available. CONCLUSION: per the predicted_effect's own stated interpretation, this null-ish result (one real instance, no more found) means recommendation (b) from cycle 70 (a server-side length/overlap guard in production) is NOT YET justified by volume on current data -- 1 instance in 98 spans (~1%) is real and worth remembering if anchor_continuation_translation is promoted out of experimental status, but does not by itself warrant adding runtime guard logic now. The detector script itself is cheap enough (pure string-length arithmetic, <1s runtime) to re-run automatically against any future soft_anchor_replay replay JSON as a standing judge()-independent regression check, which is a more actionable near-term recommendation than a production guard: suggest adding it to this repo's own experiment-review checklist for any future anchor_continuation_translation replay, rather than building guard logic against a single observed case. Per this repo's established replay/analysis-script precedent, no results.csv row added.

hypotheses.title: Does swapping which block comes first in translation_fidelity_judge()'s prompt (source-then-translation vs translation-then-source) change the retention score, on an otherwise-identical (source, translation) pair? (grounded in babeljudge2026, previously uncited)
hypotheses.description: babeljudge2026 (cycle 72 literature) measures LLM-judge reliability along four bias axes, one of which is position/order inconsistency: does a judge's verdict change when the same content is presented in a different slot order, holding the actual content constant? BabelJudge's own setup is pairwise (two candidate responses, swap which one is shown first); this repo's translation_fidelity_judge.judge(source, translation) is not pairwise -- it scores one (source, translation) pair per call -- so BabelJudge's exact method does not transfer as-is (noted in papers.json's cross_reference_check_cycle72 on babeljudge2026). Verified directly against the code before writing this (translation_fidelity_judge.py:40-63): the _JUDGE_PROMPT template is fixed to always place <source_english> before <translation_japanese>, in that order, in every call this codebase has ever made -- no experiment has ever tried the reverse order. The adaptable sub-question BabelJudge's method still supports for a non-pairwise judge is simpler and directly testable: does the ORDER of the two blocks (source-first vs translation-first) in the prompt, not their content, change the score the judge assigns to the identical (source, translation) pair? If it does, that is itself a form of position bias in this repo's judge, independent of BabelJudge's pairwise framing.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: If translation_fidelity_judge()'s score is purely a function of content (as it should be for a reliable judge), swapping block order on the identical (source, translation) pair should change the score no more than ordinary same-prompt repeat noise already measured for this judge (within_group_noise_stdev ~3.27, score-first prompt, cycle 65's h-judge-reasoning-before-score-noise). A systematic, order-correlated shift beyond that noise floor (not just random scatter) would indicate real position bias worth flagging before the judge is used for any future pairwise/ensemble comparison (e.g. the already-queued h-judge-cross-model-agreement-check). Report an honest null if the order-swapped variant's scores fall within the existing same-prompt noise floor.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/judge_block_order_replay.py that: (1) loads experiments/20260921_h_soft_anchor_gate_recalibrated_noisefloor_replay.json's by_source, restricted to zero-effect spans (gated_batch_indices == []), sampled at span_index % 4 == 0 (same stride-sampling convention as judge_reasoning_order_replay.py, ~34 span x condition groups across both source clips); (2) for each sampled group, takes repeats[0]'s last_cumulative_text as ONE fixed translation text (no new translation generation); (3) calls the EXISTING unmodified translation_fidelity_judge.judge() K=2 times per group for the current source-first prompt, and a NEW translation-first prompt variant (defined locally in the new script -- identical wording and JSON schema to _JUDGE_PROMPT, only the <source_english>/<translation_japanese> block order swapped) K=2 times on the identical fixed pair; (4) computes each variant's within-group noise stdev (reusing the same stats helper pattern as judge_reasoning_order_replay.py) AND, separately, the mean signed per-group score delta (translation_first_mean - source_first_mean) to check for a systematic directional shift, not just a noise-magnitude change. Does NOT modify translation_fidelity_judge.py itself -- the translation-first prompt stays a replay-only variant. Zero new Deepgram calls, zero new translation generation; only new spend is the judge() calls themselves. Run `uv run ruff check .` on the new file before committing.
hypotheses.result_summary: NO systematic directional position bias found in judge()'s central tendency from block order alone. On 34 sampled zero-effect span x condition groups, each judged K=2 times with the SAME fixed, already-recorded (source, translation) pair for both the current production source-first prompt and a translation-first variant (wording/schema otherwise identical), the paired per-group mean score delta (translation_first - source_first) is +1.25, but its stdev_of_deltas is 11.60 (SE~=1.99 across n=34, delta/SE~=0.63) -- the signed shift is well within noise, not distinguishable from zero. Secondary finding, smaller but real: translation_first shows moderately higher per-call scoring NOISE than source_first -- within_group_noise_stdev=5.39 vs 3.64 (~1.48x stdev, ~2.19x variance). This is in the same direction as, but notably smaller than, cycle 65's h-judge-reasoning-before-score-noise finding (reasoning-first prompt: 2.4x stdev increase over score-first on the identical design) -- both findings point the same way: deviating from translation_fidelity_judge.py's exact current wording/order tends to add judge-scoring noise rather than reduce it, at least for the two specific deviations tried so far. Conclusion: no evidence of a systematic order bias in the BabelJudge sense (a verdict that changes direction depending on presentation order), so no action needed on correctness grounds; but there is a mild noise-based argument for NOT swapping the current source-first order in production, since it is empirically the lower-noise of the two orders tested. Single K=2 check per group (not a well-powered test), consistent with this backlog's established noise-floor-before-conclusions caution (cycles 19-21).

hypotheses.title: How often does the committed JA translation output contain untranslated English source residue, beyond legitimate dictionary.csv English target terms? (grounded in failure-aware-recoverable-llm-translation-2026)
hypotheses.description: failure-aware-recoverable-llm-translation-2026 (cycle 73 literature) describes a production LLM-translation recovery protocol that includes a 'source-language residue' check: detecting when the model leaves untranslated source-language text in its output instead of translating it. Confirmed via grep (cycle 73 READ_PAPERS cross-reference) that NO equivalent check exists anywhere in this repo's production code (llm_translator.py, pipeline.py) or in any prior hypothesis/experiment. This is distinct from h-soft-anchor-truncation-detector (cycle 71, tested), which flags OUTPUTS THAT ARE TOO SHORT relative to a sibling repeat -- residue is the opposite failure shape: an output that IS the expected length but contains a verbatim or near-verbatim chunk of the English source instead of its Japanese translation. IMPORTANT CONFOUND, checked directly against dictionary.csv before finalizing this hypothesis: 46 entries have an intentionally-English (or English-containing) target_term, up to 35 characters and multi-word (e.g. 'Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)', 'Chain of Thought', 'Bag of Words') -- a naive 'flag any long run of Latin characters' detector would false-positive heavily on these legitimate, intentional terms. The detector must exclude any ASCII run that exactly matches, or is a substring of, a dictionary.csv target_term before flagging anything, and should only count it as true residue when the flagged run ALSO appears verbatim (or with high word-overlap) in that SAME event's own original_text field (same translation_complete event, not a cross-batch/cross-event comparison -- deliberately avoiding the cycle-17 caveat about original_text not being reliably cumulative ACROSS batches; this only ever compares a single event's text against its own original_text, which is a same-event field pairing, not a cross-event cumulative reconstruction).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Most experiment JSONs will show zero or near-zero true residue after dictionary-term exclusion (this repo's Gemini-based translator has not been observed to leave raw English in production use); a nonzero rate, if found, would motivate adding a lightweight residue-reject-and-retry guard to pipeline.py's translation worker, the kind of inference-time guard the source paper describes (not a training-time method, so directly portable to this repo's hosted-API architecture).
hypotheses.required_changes: New retroactive analysis script src/real_time_translation/experiments/source_residue_detector.py: for every experiment JSON under experiments/*.json with a results.events list, iterate events where kind == 'translation_complete' (committed output only, not 'translation_partial' interim text), extract maximal runs of [A-Za-z][A-Za-z '-]* (ASCII letters plus internal spaces/hyphens/apostrophes) of length >= 4 characters from the 'text' field, drop any run that exactly matches or is a substring of a dictionary.csv target_term (load dictionary.csv once), then for the remaining candidate runs check whether the run (or its word-tokenized form, allowing for case differences) appears verbatim in that SAME event's own 'original_text' field -- flag only those as true residue. Output a summary CSV/table: per-experiment residue count, and a few example flagged (original_text, text, flagged_run) triples for manual spot-check. Pure Python, no live API calls.
hypotheses.result_summary: Ran source_residue_detector.py over 25 experiment JSONs with results.events (7484 translation_complete events checked), excluding dictionary.csv target_terms. 535 candidate runs flagged (~7.1% of checked events had >=1 flagged run) -- this numerically CONTRADICTS the predicted_effect's 'near-zero true residue' expectation. BUT a word-count breakdown of the 535 flagged runs shows the predicted_effect's underlying claim (no catastrophic sentence-level source-echo failures, the specific failure mode failure-aware-recoverable-llm-translation-2026's check targets) is actually well-supported: 429/535 (80%) are single-word runs, 156 two-word, 48 three-word, and only 2 four-word (longest: 'Free Local Edge AI', 'multi model language model') -- zero flagged runs longer than 4 words, and manual inspection of every example printed to stdout shows these are overwhelmingly legitimate technical-term/proper-noun code-switching NOT present in dictionary.csv (people's names like Josh/Jessam, company/product names like Google/Salesforce/Gemini/Gemma, ML terms like 'self attention', 'speculative decoding', 'word embedding') -- exactly the kind of content real JA subtitle practice keeps in Latin script, not a translation failure. CONCLUSION: the naive 'any dictionary-excluded ASCII run that also appears in original_text' detector design does not distinguish single/short-phrase proper-noun code-switching (expected, benign) from genuine clause-level source-language residue (the paper's actual target failure mode) -- it needs a word-count floor (e.g. >=5 words) to be a useful signal. Re-running with that floor on this same data finds ZERO flagged events, i.e. this pipeline shows no evidence of the catastrophic failure mode the source paper describes, at least across these 25 clips. Marking TESTED, not ABANDONED: the detector itself is sound infrastructure (correctly dictionary-aware, same-event-only comparison, zero false positives at the long-run end) and is worth keeping as a regression check for future experiments, but this cycle's specific hypothesis (meaningful residue exists) is NOT supported by the data. Secondary observation (not pursued further this cycle, depth-over-breadth): many of the flagged single/two-word technical terms (chatbot, embedding, multilayer perceptron, word embedding, etc.) recur across multiple clips and are not in dictionary.csv -- a future hypothesis could ask whether adding them improves translation consistency, independent of the residue-detector angle.

hypotheses.title: When dictionary.csv specifies a Japanese target_term for an English source_term, does the LLM actually use it, or does the English source term sometimes leak through untranslated? (grounded_in failure-aware-recoverable-llm-translation-2026, direct follow-up of h-translation-source-residue-detector's own output)
hypotheses.description: h-translation-source-residue-detector (cycle 73) concluded 'no catastrophic source-language residue', but that conclusion only separated flagged runs by word count (<=4 words = assumed benign code-switching). Re-inspecting its own output JSON (experiments/20261024_h_translation_source_residue_detector.json) found a case that word-count filtering mislabels: the dictionary.csv entry 'language model' -> '言語モデル' (source_term 'language model', a genuinely Japanese target_term, NOT one of the 46 intentional-English-anchor entries like RoPE/Chain of Thought) is flagged as residue 6 times across the llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict experiment alone, verified by reading the actual original_text/text pairs directly (not just the aggregate count): e.g. original_text 'language model efficiency...' -> committed text 'language modelの効率性について...' -- the English source string appears verbatim where the dictionary says 言語モデル should be, with Japanese particles/grammar correctly wrapped around the untranslated English noun. This is a DIFFERENT failure shape from the code-switching the cycle-73 analysis correctly waved off (a proper noun/brand name like 'Google' has no dictionary.csv entry mandating a Japanese translation at all, so leaving it in English is not a compliance failure; 'language model' has an explicit, unambiguous, pre-existing dictionary mapping the LLM is simply not following in these instances). The open question this hypothesis tests: how common is this specific failure mode -- a dictionary entry whose target_term is Japanese (not an intentional-English entry) being bypassed in favor of the literal English source_term -- across the full experiment corpus and across dictionary entries, not just this one observed case of 'language model'.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Compliance (target_term used when source_term's English form appears in original_text) will be high overall (dictionary injection works for most entries/occurrences) but measurably below 100% for at least a handful of entries, 'language model' being the already-confirmed example; if a pattern emerges (e.g. compliance drops specifically when the source term appears mid-sentence embedded in a longer clause vs. as an isolated noun phrase, or drops for terms that are also common standalone English words), that would motivate a concrete prompt-engineering fix (e.g. reformatting the dictionary block, or emphasizing compliance in the system prompt) rather than a vague 'dictionary isn't perfect' conclusion.
hypotheses.required_changes: New retroactive analysis script src/real_time_translation/experiments/dictionary_compliance_checker.py: load dictionary.csv, split entries into 'translated' (target_term contains at least one Japanese character -- hiragana/katakana/kanji unicode ranges, re.search(r'[\u3040-\u30ff\u4e00-\u9fff]', target_term)) vs 'intentional-English-anchor' (target_term has no Japanese characters at all, e.g. RoPE/Chain of Thought -- excluded from this check, they are correctly-English by design). For each 'translated' entry, scan every experiment JSON's translation_complete events (same same-event original_text/text field pairing as source_residue_detector.py -- never cross-event) for occurrences of the source_term (case-insensitive, word-boundary regex) in original_text. For each such occurrence, classify the paired text field as 'compliant' (the Japanese target_term, or a close variant, appears in text), 'leaked' (the literal English source_term string appears verbatim in text instead), or 'ambiguous' (neither clearly present -- e.g. the sentence was reworded enough that neither string appears literally; log these separately, do not count them as compliant or leaked). Output a per-entry and overall compliance-rate table plus example (original_text, text) triples for every leaked occurrence, to the same experiments/*.csv + experiments/*.json sidecar convention as source_residue_detector.py. Pure Python, reads existing experiments/*.json and dictionary.csv only -- no live API calls.
hypotheses.result_summary: Prediction confirmed. Of 30 dictionary.csv entries with a genuinely Japanese target_term, only 4 (attention, language model, backpropagation, classification) actually occurred in any experiment's original_text; across those, 458 occurrences (compliant=380, leaked=29, ambiguous=49), overall compliance rate 92.91% (compliant/(compliant+leaked)) -- measurably below 100%, confirming the predicted leak exists at a non-trivial rate, concentrated in 2 entries: 'attention' (20/133 leaked, 84.6% compliant) and 'language model' (9/317 leaked, 96.7% compliant). A real implementation bug was caught and fixed mid-analysis before trusting these numbers: the initial \b-word-boundary regex silently undercounted leaks (6 instead of 29) because Python's \w/\b treat Japanese kana/kanji as word characters, so an English term immediately abutting Japanese text with no space (e.g. 'attentionを行います') has no \b boundary and was misclassified 'ambiguous' instead of 'leaked' -- fixed with an ASCII-only lookaround boundary, verified empirically (same playbook lesson as cycles 13/17/20/66/73). The second part of the predicted_effect also holds: nearly all leaked 'attention' occurrences are the compound phrase 'self attention' (a term not itself in dictionary.csv, only its head noun is), i.e. compliance drops specifically when the dictionary term is embedded inside a longer noun phrase/clause rather than standing alone -- a concrete, actionable pattern, not just 'dictionary isn't perfect'. 'language model' leaks cluster heavily in one experiment (llm2025_ep8_zenhan_full_lecture_v2_dict, 7/9), consistent with topic density (a lecture almost entirely about language models) rather than a different per-entry mechanism. No prompt-engineering fix was implemented this cycle (out of scope for a $0 retroactive-analysis hypothesis); the concrete next step is a human-reviewable candidate for h-review-* style follow-up: either add compound forms (e.g. 'self attention' -> 'セルフアテンション') as their own dictionary.csv entries, or test a system-prompt instruction emphasizing dictionary compliance even when the term appears inside a longer phrase.

hypotheses.title: Can the completeness signal h-semantic-completeness-gating used a SEPARATE classifier call for be folded into the SAME translation call instead, removing the second API call entirely? (grounded_in cuhksz2026-iwslt-qwen3omni-wait-token)
hypotheses.description: cuhksz2026-iwslt-qwen3omni-wait-token (IWSLT 2026) bakes its streaming read/write decision directly into the model's own generation (wait tokens emitted as part of the output), rather than using a separate policy module. This repo's own h-semantic-completeness-gating (cycle ~17) tried a conceptually adjacent idea but implemented it as a SEPARATE, non-translation classifier call (LLMTranslator.check_completeness, wired into DeepgramTranscriber's force-finalize loop via pipeline.py's _gated_completeness_check, see pipeline.py around the '# Rate limiter shared across all translation workers AND the semantic-completeness-gating classifier below' comment). That hypothesis's own result_summary reports the mechanism worked correctly (one span's cross-batch NE went from 3.0 to a perfect 0.0 when the gate fired early) but overall latency got WORSE, and pipeline.py's own comment attributes this to the completeness check competing for the same rate-limited API quota as real translation calls -- an architectural cost of using a second call, not evidence the underlying idea is wrong. cuhksz's paper suggests the fix without fine-tuning: since this repo's translation call is already itself an LLM API call, ask that SAME call to also return a structured 'is this source text so far semantically complete, or does it look like it will obviously continue' field (e.g. one extra boolean field in the existing structured-output translation response) instead of issuing check_completeness as a second, separate request. This removes the second call's rate-limit contention entirely by construction, which is the one concrete factor h-semantic-completeness-gating's own analysis named as the regression's likely cause.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: A combined single-call completeness signal will (a) agree with the existing separate-classifier check_completeness's historical True/False decisions on already-recorded ASR interim texts at a high rate (it is answering the same semantic question), and (b) by construction eliminate the second API call per check, removing the specific rate-limit-contention mechanism h-semantic-completeness-gating's result_summary blamed for its latency regression -- though this hypothesis can only test (a) via replay against already-recorded text; (b)'s actual latency effect requires a live run (see required_changes) and is NOT claimed as proven by the replay alone.
hypotheses.required_changes: CORRECTED during RUN_EXPERIMENTS (cycle 75) after reading the actual data/code -- the original required_changes text above assumed two things that turned out false: (1) h-semantic-completeness-gating's experiment JSONs (experiments/20260917_h_semantic_gating_test_v2.json) do NOT log the check_completeness classifier's per-call True/False decisions anywhere -- only asr_interim events' growing partial-source-text snapshots (91 available) are recorded, confirmed by reading the JSON's events list directly; (2) translate_stream has NO structured-output schema at all (it is a plain streamed-text call, confirmed by reading llm_translator.py directly) -- there is no existing JSON field to additively extend. Corrected plan: new script src/real_time_translation/experiments/combined_completeness_signal_replay.py. For a stride-sampled subset of the asr_interim growing-text snapshots, issue TWO fresh calls per snapshot (no reuse of any logged decision, since none exists): (1) the EXISTING separate check_completeness prompt, replicated inline with the same wording as llm_translator.py's _COMPLETENESS_PROMPT_TEMPLATE -> True/False/None; (2) a NEW combined prompt asking the model to produce the Japanese translation of the same text AND a trailing <completeness>COMPLETE|INCOMPLETE</completeness> tag in one response (an ad-hoc delimiter convention for this experiment only, NOT a change to production code/schema). Compare the two calls' completeness verdicts for agreement. Pure replay against gemini-3-flash-preview (the real translation model), zero new Deepgram spend, zero live ASR.
hypotheses.result_summary: Prediction (a) confirmed, prediction (b) correctly left untested (as scoped). combined_completeness_signal_replay.py sampled 31 growing asr_interim text snapshots (stride 3 of 91 available) from experiments/20260917_h_semantic_gating_test_v2.json and issued two fresh gemini-3-flash-preview calls per snapshot: the existing separate check_completeness prompt, and a new combined translate+<completeness> tag call. RESULT: 31/31 (100%) agreement between the two verdicts, with genuine variance in the underlying answers (27 INCOMPLETE, 4 COMPLETE -- not a degenerate all-one-answer case), and zero unparseable responses from either call format (num_either_none=0), confirming the ad-hoc <translation>/<completeness> delimiter format is robust enough to parse reliably at this sample size. This supports the premise that a single combined call CAN carry the same completeness signal as the current separate classifier call, with no accuracy cost observed. Caveat stated honestly: n=31 from one 90s clip is a small, single-clip sample -- not a claim this generalizes to all speech styles/domains. More importantly, this replay deliberately did NOT test the actual production question this hypothesis was motivated by (whether removing the second call fixes h-semantic-completeness-gating's observed latency regression): that regression was attributed to the separate classifier call competing for shared rate-limited API capacity against real translation calls, and a live measurement of that effect needs an actual pipeline.py-integrated A/B (combined call replacing both the gate check AND the eventual translation call), not a replay issuing two independent calls per snapshot as done here. NEXT STEP (not in this hypothesis's scope, would need its own HUMAN_APPROVAL since it touches pipeline.py's live force-finalize path): implement the combined-call format as an actual alternative code path in llm_translator.py and pipeline.py, and run a live A/B against h-semantic-completeness-gating's original baseline to measure the real latency/call-count effect this hypothesis was ultimately trying to motivate.

hypotheses.title: Does asking translation_fidelity_judge for the decomposed rubric fields alongside the holistic score make that SAME holistic score noisier across repeats, per unlp2026's human-rater finding that decomposed rating is LESS reliable than pure holistic rating? (grounded_in unlp2026-holistic-vs-decomposed-scale)
hypotheses.description: unlp2026-holistic-vs-decomposed-scale (a human-rater study, 8 professional EN->UK translators) found the OPPOSITE of the usual 'decomposition reduces noise' assumption: a holistic single 0-100 score gave significantly HIGHER inter-rater reliability than a decomposed fluency+adequacy protocol, for both human and LLM judges tested. Its own key_findings explicitly flag that this cuts against the direction this repo's h-judge-rubric-decomposition-schematic-adherence (cycle 53) took -- moving judge() from a single holistic score toward a 5-field decomposed rubric (judge_decomposed() in judge_schematic_adherence_replay.py) on the unexamined assumption that decomposition helps. That cycle's own replay was INCONCLUSIVE on the related factor-collapse question (not this noise question) because it sampled from spans with a severe ceiling effect (causal_logical_relationships=100 for 60/60 points) -- its own result_summary names 'a future replay should sample from spans/sources with documented fidelity cost/variation instead (e.g. h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction's ... experiment JSONs ...)' as the concrete next step. This hypothesis takes that exact next step, but asks a different, more directly testable question than factor-collapse: does the holistic 'score' field ITSELF get noisier (higher repeat-to-repeat variance on an identical, unchanged input) when the judge is also asked to produce 4 other named sub-criteria in the same response (judge_decomposed), versus asked for only the holistic score alone (judge())? This is the LLM-judge analogue of unlp2026's human-rater reliability comparison -- not a literal replication (unlp2026 compared decomposed-then-aggregate scoring against pure holistic scoring across independent human raters; here the comparison is one single-field judge prompt vs. a second prompt that asks for the same holistic field embedded alongside 4 sub-criteria in one response), but the closest testable instance available in this repo's existing judge infrastructure, and a second, independent line of evidence for the same general claim if the direction matches.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Per unlp2026's finding, predict decomposed_embedded_holistic_noise > holistic_only_noise -- the holistic 'score' asked for alongside 4 other sub-criteria (judge_decomposed) is less stable across repeats on an identical input than the same holistic judgment asked for alone (judge()). A null or reversed result (no difference, or judge_decomposed's embedded score is actually less noisy) is equally worth reporting honestly -- this is a small-n (8 points x 3 repeats x 2 variants = 48 calls) exploratory check on one clip, not a definitive test, and any aggregate ratio must be read with the same caution PLAYBOOK.md's ANALYZE_RESULTS section already requires for judge-noise comparisons (cycles 19-22: a small aggregate difference can be noise, not signal, unless it clears an explicitly-computed per-point variance floor -- do not pool raw scores across points before computing that floor).
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/judge_holistic_vs_decomposed_noise.py. Sample points: 8 segments from experiments/20260916_compression_actions_prompt.json's results['compression_actions']['segments'] list (verified directly: 23 segments, each with 'index'/'source_text'/'translation' fields) -- segment index 5 (h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction's own result_summary documents this as a genuine, confirmed dropped-content case: baseline translated the clause in full, compression_actions truncated it mid-clause) plus 7 more stride-sampled segments (index % 3 == 0, i.e. 0,3,6,9,12,15,18,21, picking 7 of these distinct from index 5) for diversity, specifically to avoid the all-ceiling-effect failure mode that made h-judge-rubric-decomposition-schematic-adherence's replay inconclusive. For each sampled (source_text, translation) pair, call the EXISTING translation_fidelity_judge.judge() (unmodified, holistic-only prompt) K=3 times, and the EXISTING judge_schematic_adherence_replay.judge_decomposed() (unmodified, decomposed-plus-holistic-score prompt) K=3 times -- import and reuse both functions as-is, do not duplicate either prompt string. For each point, compute the within-point sample variance (via stats.stdev, squared, for repo convention) of judge()'s 'score' across its 3 repeats, and separately of judge_decomposed()'s 'score' field across its own 3 repeats. Aggregate across the 8 points into one pooled noise estimate per variant as sqrt(mean of per-point variances) -- per PLAYBOOK.md's ANALYZE_RESULTS rule and judge_noise_power_analysis.py's established convention, not a naive concatenated stdev across points. Also report stats.mean of each variant's scores per point as a sanity check that neither variant is degenerate (all-identical) by construction, and flag explicitly if either variant hits the same ceiling-effect failure mode as cycle 53 (near-zero within-point variance for most points) -- if so, treat the result as inconclusive for the SAME reason as cycle 53, not as evidence of 'no noise difference'. Write experiments/judge_holistic_vs_decomposed_noise.json + a results.csv row per CLAUDE.md/PLAYBOOK.md logging convention. Run `uv run ruff check .` (or the `python3 -m ruff check <path>` venv workaround if `uv run` hits the zoom/rtms test.pypi.org sync block) before committing.
hypotheses.result_summary: INCONCLUSIVE, dominated by a ceiling effect on the holistic-only side. Ran judge_holistic_vs_decomposed_noise.py: 8 sampled (source_text, translation) pairs from experiments/20260916_compression_actions_prompt.json (index 5 plus stride-3 indices 0,3,6,9,12,15,18) x judge() (holistic-only) vs judge_decomposed() (decomposed-plus-holistic) x 3 repeats each = 48 live gemini-3.1-flash-lite calls. judge() returned the IDENTICAL score on all 3 repeats for 8/8 sampled points (pooled noise stdev=0.0); judge_decomposed() showed nonzero variance on 2/8 points (index 3: [20,30,30], index 9: [80,100,100]), pooled noise stdev=4.56. The direction matches unlp2026s prediction (decomposed > holistic noise) but a variant at a hard floor of zero variance on every single point cannot be compared meaningfully to any nonzero number -- same failure mode PLAYBOOK.md ANALYZE_RESULTS already documents from cycle 53s replay (near-ceiling segments give no signal to compare). Root cause: this clips compression_actions segments mostly score 90-100 deterministically; only index 3 (score ~40) showed any real judge disagreement at all, in EITHER variant. Do not read this as "holistic-only has zero noise" -- it means this sample has no headroom to show noise. Concrete next step for a future replay: resample from segments/sources with more marginal or contested content (lower baseline scores, more genuine translation imperfection) instead of this clip -- e.g. revisit the guest-talk clip used by h-soft-anchor-generalization-guest-talk/h-soft-anchor-disfluency-gate (experiments/20260915_llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min_rpm60.json), which cycle 21s noise-floor work already showed has higher between-span variance (translation difficulty varies more) than this clip.

hypotheses.title: Does this repo's soft-anchor disfluency gate (GATE_MIN_WORDS) fire almost entirely on utterance-final batches, where by construction no future audio can arrive to justify holding back -- the same 'temporally-blind over-reading' pathology reina-santan2026-readwrite-overread-bias identifies in trained SimulST read/write policies? (grounded_in reina-santan2026-readwrite-overread-bias)
hypotheses.description: reina-santan2026-readwrite-overread-bias's core critique of pure information-gain read/write policies is that they lack temporal context: they keep 'reading' (holding back a decision) even when no further reading can actually help, biasing the whole system toward late, over-cautious commits. This repo's soft_anchor_disfluency_gate_replay.py implements its own small read/write-style decision for a different purpose (anchoring quality) but with an analogous structure: `gated = i > 0 and len(batch.delta_text.split()) < GATE_MIN_WORDS` (soft_anchor_disfluency_gate_replay.py:83) decides, per batch, whether to hold back (fall back to a from-scratch re-translation instead of anchoring) based purely on the batch's own word count -- with zero awareness of whether more audio/context is actually still coming for that utterance. A quick check this cycle (python3 one-liner over the two existing gated-condition experiment JSONs, counting `batches[idx]['is_utterance_end']` for every index in each span's `gated_batch_indices`) found the gate fires almost exclusively on exactly the LAST batch of its utterance: 22/22 (100%) in experiments/20260921_h_soft_anchor_gate_recalibrated_noisefloor_replay.json, 46/47 (97.9%) in experiments/20260922_h_soft_anchor_gate_min3_replay.json. This is architecturally unsurprising (a short trailing delta_text, e.g. a single leftover word like 'your', is more likely to be an utterance's final fragment than a mid-utterance chunk) but has not previously been measured or connected to the gate's known cost: h_soft_anchor_gate_erasure_decomposition (2026-10-10, retroactive, already in experiments/soft_anchor_gate_erasure_decomposition.json) found gated_soft_anchor's excess normalized erasure over soft_anchor_replay is 0.549 on gated transitions themselves (n=84, mean_norm 0.615 vs 0.067) -- a real, already-confirmed cost -- but that analysis never checked whether this cost is concentrated on is_utterance_end batches specifically, nor whether the gate buys any compensating judge-score/fidelity benefit on exactly that subset where, per reina-santan2026's framing, the gate's own rationale (hold back because more disambiguating context may still arrive) cannot structurally apply (there is no more audio left in the utterance).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Per reina-santan2026's temporal-blindness framing, predict that formalizing this cycle's quick check across both existing gated-condition experiment JSONs confirms the gate fires overwhelmingly (>=95%) on is_utterance_end=true batches, and that gated_soft_anchor shows no judge-score/fidelity improvement over soft_anchor_replay on that exact subset (using the correct per-span noise-floor method from judge_noise_power_analysis.py's `_decompose_zero_effect_variance`, not a pooled concatenation, per PLAYBOOK.md's ANALYZE_RESULTS rules -- h_soft_anchor_gate_erasure_decomposition already showed the NE cost is real, so this hypothesis is specifically about whether there is an offsetting quality benefit on this subset, not about re-measuring the cost itself). A null or reversed result (the gate does show a measurable quality benefit even on utterance-final batches) is equally worth reporting -- it would mean the gate's value isn't really about 'waiting for more context' at all, which would itself be a useful correction to how this gate's rationale has been described in prior cycles' hypothesis text.
